course.title: Linear Algebra: Vectors and Maps
course.description: Move vectors, reshape a plane and fit noisy measurements. Build up to eigenvectors and singular value decomposition.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with signed arithmetic, simple equations and coordinate graphs. Work with real vectors and small matrices through rectangular SVD.

paragraphs: Linear algebra studies lists of numbers, called vectors, and the tables of numbers, called matrices, that act on them. A vector such as (4, 1) can describe a position, a displacement or a force, and a matrix can stretch, turn or flatten every vector in the plane at once, so that a single table of four numbers describes what happens to infinitely many arrows.

Linear algebra restricts itself to maps that respect adding and scaling, which are called linear, and such a map is settled completely by what it does to a few vectors: once you know where (1, 0) and (0, 1) are sent, you know where every vector in the plane goes. That is why a small table of numbers is enough to describe a rotation, a reflection or a stretch of the whole plane, and why asking which input produced a given output becomes a system of equations that a fixed procedure can solve.

Because a linear map is a table of numbers, its structure can be read from the numbers. Some directions are only stretched by a map and never turned, and these directions and their stretch factors show what the map does in its simplest terms, while a measurement problem with no exact solution can be answered by the nearest approximate one, as when a line is fitted to noisy data. Ideas of this kind run through computer graphics, physics, statistics and machine learning, which is why linear algebra is the standard language for reasoning about many numbers together.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a vector, add and scale vectors, and find a length or a dot product.
You'll be able to apply a matrix to a vector and say what it does to the plane.
You'll be able to solve a small system of equations by row reduction and say how many solutions it has.
You'll be able to find a determinant, a projection and a least-squares fit for small examples.
You'll be able to find the eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 matrix and read what a singular value decomposition reports.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with signed arithmetic, simple equations and reading points on a coordinate graph.

lessons.title: Read a vector

steps.headline: A vector is a list of numbers whose order says what each one means

lead.text: The pair in the figure has two parts, and what each part means is settled by where it stands. The first number says how far to go across, to the right, and the second says how far to go up, so (4, 1) is 4 across and 1 up. A list of numbers read in this way is called a **vector**, and each number in it is a **coordinate**, named *x* for the first and *y* for the second.
The explorer draws a vector as an arrow from the starting corner, (0, 0), which is called the **origin**, to the place the two coordinates name.

afterFigure.text: Switch to (2, 3) and the arrow ends somewhere else, because both coordinates have changed. **The position of a number in the list decides which direction it measures**, and that is why the list needs no labels. Lists with more entries follow the same rule, but most of this course draws the two-coordinate kind, since it can be shown on a page.

steps.headline: A minus sign sends the arrow the other way

lead.text: Coordinates are not always positive. A negative first coordinate means going to the *left* instead of the right, and a negative second coordinate means going down instead of up. The vector (−3, 2) therefore runs 3 to the left and 2 up, while (5, −1) runs 5 to the right and 1 down, and the explorer shows both.

afterFigure.text: The sign belongs to its number and travels with it. A coordinate of −3 is not a smaller kind of 3, and it is not a subtraction waiting for something to be taken away: it is the instruction to go 3 units in the opposite direction. **The size of a coordinate says how far, and its sign says which way.**

steps.headline: Reading the coordinates of (−4, 1)

lead.text: The minus sign in (−4, 1) makes it tempting to treat the 4 as smaller than the 1, so name the two coordinates one position at a time.

workedSteps.text: The first coordinate is the number written first, and its sign is part of it. The arrow goes 4 units to the left.
The second coordinate is the number written second. The arrow goes 1 unit up.
Together the two coordinates describe an arrow that runs 4 to the left and 1 up from the origin.

lead.text: A single letter such as *v* is often used to name a vector.

steps.headline: Two vectors are equal only when every coordinate matches

lead.text: Swapping the two coordinates of (2, 6) gives (6, 2), which uses the same numbers and yet names a different place. The first arrow climbs 6 units while moving only 2 across, and the second travels 6 across and rises only 2. The figure draws both from the origin, so their ends can be compared directly.

afterFigure.text: Because each position has its own meaning, two vectors are the same only when their first coordinates agree *and* their second coordinates agree. Having the same numbers in a different order is not enough, which is why a vector is called an **ordered** list.

steps.headline: Are (3, 7) and (7, 3) the same vector?

lead.text: Apply the rule to a new pair of vectors, comparing one position at a time.

workedSteps.text: Write the two vectors with their coordinates in position.
Compare the coordinates position by position: the first coordinates are 3 and 7, and the second are 7 and 3.
Decide whether the two are the same vector.

steps.headline: A vector can also be a move, and the zero vector is a move that goes nowhere

lead.text: So far every vector has started at the origin, which makes it a way of naming a place. The same pair also describes a *move*: (4, 1) means 4 across and 1 up from wherever you happen to be, and the move is the same size whether it begins at the origin or somewhere else. A vector records how far and in which direction to go and says nothing about where the journey starts, whereas a single number with no direction attached, such as 3 or −2, is called a **scalar**.

One vector has no direction at all. The vector (0, 0) says 0 across and 0 up, so it leaves you exactly where you began, and it is called the **zero vector**. Every other vector has at least one coordinate that is not zero, and **a coordinate of zero means no movement in that direction**.

lessons.orientation: Read signed coordinates and distinguish vectors from individual scalars.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The pair (4, 1) names a place. Starting from a corner of a grid, go 4 units along the bottom and then 1 unit up, and you arrive at the point the pair describes. The two numbers cannot be swapped, because (1, 4) leads to a different place, which means that the order of the numbers is part of what the pair says, and a list of numbers with that property is called a vector.

Every later operation in the course, from adding two vectors to applying a matrix to one, takes pairs like this as its input, so reading a pair correctly is the skill that the rest depends on. A pair can stand for a position, as here, or for a move of that many units across and up from wherever you happen to be, and in both readings it is the position of each number in the pair that tells you what it means.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the coordinates of a vector, including negative ones, and see why their order matters.
intro.whyItMatters: Every operation later in the course begins by reading coordinates correctly.

recap.keyIdea: A vector is an ordered list of coordinates: the first says how far across, the second how far up, and a minus sign reverses the direction.

blocks.text: A vector such as (−4, 1) is read by position, with the sign kept as part of each coordinate, so it runs 4 to the left and 1 up. Two vectors are equal only when every coordinate matches, which makes (1, 4) and (4, 1) different, and the zero vector (0, 0) is the move that goes nowhere.

recap.nextHook: Next, two moves made one after another combine into a single vector, and a number can stretch or reverse a vector.

lessons.title: Add and scale vectors

steps.headline: Adding vectors adds their matching coordinates

lead.text: Take the moves (3, 1) and (2, 2). The first goes 3 across and 1 up, and the second then goes a further 2 across and 2 up, so the total distance across is 3 + 2 = 5 and the total distance up is 1 + 2 = 3. The single move that does the work of both is (5, 3), which is called the **sum** of the two vectors and is written (3, 1) + (2, 2) = (5, 3). **Adding vectors means adding the matching coordinates**, the first with the first and the second with the second.
The explorer draws the two moves end to end, with the sum as the arrow from the start to the finish. The second case changes the second move to (−2, 2), which sends the path back towards the left.

afterFigure.text: A negative coordinate simply subtracts. Across the whole path of the second case, 3 + (−2) = 1, so the path finishes *only* 1 across, even though the first move alone went 3. Ordinary addition does not depend on order, and neither does this: doing (2, 2) first and (3, 1) second would finish at the same point, (5, 3).

steps.headline: Subtracting vectors gives the move from one point to another

lead.text: The same rule works with a minus sign: **subtract the matching coordinates**, in the order written. The figure marks two points, Q = (2, 1) and P = (6, 4), each reached from the origin by its own arrow. The move that goes from Q to P is the difference P − Q = (6 − 2, 4 − 1) = (4, 3).

afterFigure.text: Order matters here, in a way it did not for addition. Going from Q to P is 4 across and 3 up, while going from P back to Q is Q − P = (−4, −3), the same journey in reverse. A difference is best read as *end minus start*: the move from one point to another has the coordinates of where it finishes less those of where it began.

steps.headline: Multiplying a vector by a number multiplies every coordinate

lead.text: Making the same move three times in a row, (1, 2) and then (1, 2) and then (1, 2), gives (1 + 1 + 1, 2 + 2 + 2) = (3, 6), which is three times each coordinate. A number used in this way to stretch a vector is a [[scalar|A single number with no direction attached. Met in 'Read a vector'.]], and the result is written 3(1, 2) = (3, 6). The explorer shows it beside the case of a scalar between 0 and 1, where ½(1, 2) = (½, 1) is half as long and points the same way.

afterFigure.text: Both coordinates must be multiplied. If only one were, the arrow would swing round to a new direction, whereas **scaling stretches the arrow along its own line**. Multiplying by a positive scalar changes the *length* of a vector and never its direction.

steps.headline: Triple the vector (2, −1)

lead.text: Scaling works one coordinate at a time. The first coordinate is done for you, and the second is yours.

workedSteps.text: Write the product, with the scalar outside the brackets.
Multiply the first coordinate by 3.
Multiply the second coordinate by 3. Its sign stays with it.

steps.headline: A negative scalar reverses the vector

lead.text: A scalar of −1 gives (−1)(1, 2) = (−1, −2). Every coordinate changes sign, so the arrow has the same length and points exactly the other way. A scalar of −3 does the same and stretches as well, giving (−3, −6), an arrow three times as long that points backwards, and the explorer shows both.

afterFigure.text: A scalar therefore does two separate jobs: its *size* sets the length, and its *sign* sets whether the direction is kept or reversed. This also explains subtraction, because u − v is the same as u + (−1)v, the vector u added to the reverse of v. **Every difference can be rewritten as a sum.**

steps.headline: A calculation may scale some vectors and then add them

lead.text: The two operations can be used together, as in 2(1, 3) + (4, −2). The usual rules of arithmetic apply, so a number multiplying a vector binds more tightly than a plus sign, and **the scaling is done first** and the addition second. The figure shows this: (1, 3) is doubled to (2, 6), and then (4, −2) is added, which takes the path to (6, 4).

afterFigure.text: A sum of scaled vectors in this form is called a **linear combination**. It is the idea to which the rest of the course keeps returning, in the guise of matrices, spans and bases, so it is worth being sure of the order: scale *each* vector, then add the results.

lead.text: Scale first and add second, one coordinate at a time.

workedSteps.text: Multiply both coordinates of the first vector by 2.
Add the matching coordinates of that result and the second vector: 6 + (−1) across and 2 + 4 up.
The combination is a single vector.

lessons.orientation: Combine displacements, scale every coordinate and handle negative scalars.

blocks.text: Take two moves, (2, 1) and then (1, 2), where each pair says how far to go across and how far to go up. The second move starts where the first ended, so together they trace a path with a bend in it and leave you 3 across and 3 up from where you began. A single move of (3, 3) would have taken you to the same place, which means that two moves can always be replaced by one, and finding that one is what it means to add vectors.

Repeating one move several times leads to the second operation, multiplying a vector by a number, which stretches the move along its own line. With these two operations a vector can be combined with others to reach new places, and nearly everything later in linear algebra, from the action of a matrix to the solution of a system, can be described as combining vectors in this way.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add and subtract vectors, multiply a vector by a number, and combine the two operations in one calculation.
intro.whyItMatters: Adding and scaling are the operations that every later idea, from matrices to eigenvectors, is built from.

recap.keyIdea: Vectors add and subtract coordinate by coordinate, and multiplying by a scalar multiplies every coordinate.

blocks.text: Adding two vectors chains their moves end to end and gives the single move with the same result, found by adding matching coordinates. A scalar stretches a vector along its own line, a negative scalar also reverses it, and in a calculation such as 2u + v the scaling comes first, because a sum of scaled vectors is a linear combination.

recap.nextHook: Next, a different product of two vectors, which multiplies matching coordinates and adds the results, measures how closely two vectors point the same way.

lessons.title: Dot products and length

steps.headline: The length of a vector comes from Pythagoras's theorem

lead.text: Take the vector (8, 15). Its two coordinates are the sides of a right-angled triangle, with a horizontal side of 8 and a vertical side of 15, and the arrow itself is the long side opposite the right angle. Pythagoras's theorem, which Euclid proved in Book I of the *Elements*, says that the square on the long side equals the sum of the squares on the other two, so the arrow's length is the square root of 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289, which is 17.
That number is called the **length** of the vector, and it is written with double bars, so that in general the vector (a, b) has length:

afterFigure.text: The coordinates enter only through their squares, so a change of sign does not change the length. The second case in the explorer, (−15, 8), also has length 17, since 225 + 64 is again 289. **A length is never negative**, and it is zero only for the zero vector, where both squares are zero.

steps.headline: The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the results

lead.text: A second calculation uses two vectors. To find the **dot product** of (5, 1) and (2, 3), multiply the matching coordinates and add the results: 5 × 2 + 1 × 3 = 10 + 3 = 13. It is written with a dot between the vectors, so (5, 1) · (2, 3) = 13, and in general:

The answer is a single number rather than a vector, which is why the dot product is also called the scalar product, and nothing changes for longer lists except that each further pair of coordinates adds one more product to the sum. The notation with a dot comes from Josiah Willard Gibbs, who printed his *Elements of Vector Analysis* for his students at Yale in 1881 and 1884.

steps.headline: The sign of a dot product shows whether two vectors point the same way

lead.text: A dot product can be positive, negative or zero, and the sign says something about direction. The explorer dots the vector (3, 1) with (1, 2), which points broadly the *same* way, and then with (−1, −2), which points the opposite way. The first gives 3 × 1 + 1 × 2 = 5, and the second gives 3 × (−1) + 1 × (−2) = −5.

afterFigure.text: The pattern is general: **the dot product is positive when two vectors point broadly the same way, and negative when they point broadly opposite ways**. The exact statement is u · v = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors, so the sign is the sign of cos θ, positive for angles below 90° and negative for angles above it. Each product in the sum can itself be negative, so the signs of the coordinates have to be carried through the arithmetic with care.

steps.headline: The length of (−7, 24)

lead.text: A minus sign in a coordinate looks as though it should change the length, so square first and take the root last.

workedSteps.text: Square each coordinate. The square of −7 is a positive number.
Add the squares.
Take the square root of the sum.

steps.headline: The dot product of (2, 1) and (3, −2)

lead.text: The two products are laid out, and adding them is your part.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the first coordinates.
Multiply the second coordinates. One of them is negative, so the product is too.
Add the two products to get the dot product.

steps.headline: A vector dotted with itself is its length squared

lead.text: Dot a vector with itself and each product becomes a square: (3, 4) · (3, 4) = 3 × 3 + 4 × 4 = 9 + 16 = 25. That is the number under the root in the length formula, and the length of (3, 4) is √25 = 5, so in general **v · v = ‖v‖²** and the length can be written ‖v‖ = √(v · v).

This ties the two calculations of the lesson together. It also shows why a vector's dot product with itself is *never* negative, since it is a sum of squares, and why it is zero only for the zero vector. Distance in the plane and the dot product are the same arithmetic seen from two sides, which later lessons use to measure lengths and angles from coordinates alone.

lessons.orientation: Use matching-coordinate products to measure alignment and vector length.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The vector (3, 4) ends 3 units across and 4 units up, and the straight arrow from the origin to its tip has a definite length. Adding the coordinates gives 7, but that is the distance along the two sides of the right-angled corner, and the arrow that cuts across the corner is shorter. The coordinates fix the tip exactly, so they must fix the length as well, and one calculation on them recovers it.

A close relative of that calculation takes two vectors, multiplies their matching coordinates and adds the results. The number it produces measures how closely the two vectors point the same way, so that both questions, how long a vector is and which way it points, can be answered by arithmetic on the coordinates alone.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the length of a vector and the dot product of two vectors, and say what the sign of a dot product tells you.
intro.whyItMatters: Length and the dot product are how coordinates answer questions about distance and direction.

recap.keyIdea: The length of a vector is the square root of the sum of its squared coordinates, and the dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds.

blocks.text: A vector's length follows from Pythagoras's theorem, and equals the square root of its dot product with itself. The dot product of two different vectors is a single number whose sign shows whether they point broadly together, with a positive value, or broadly apart, with a negative one.

recap.nextHook: Next, the borderline case: a dot product of exactly zero, and the vectors of length 1 that make directions easy to compare.

lessons.title: Orthogonal and unit vectors

steps.headline: Dividing a vector by its length gives a vector of length 1

lead.text: Take the vector (8, 15), whose [[length|The square root of the sum of the squared coordinates. Met in 'Dot products and length'.]] is 17. Dividing every coordinate by 17 gives (8/17, 15/17). Scaling by a positive number *never* changes direction, so the new vector points the same way as the old, and its length has become 17 times smaller: the squares add to (64 + 225)/289 = 1. A vector of length 1 is a **unit vector**, and dividing a nonzero vector by its own length to obtain one is called **normalising** it.

lead.latex: \frac{v}{\lVert v \rVert}\ \text{has length } 1 \text{ and points the same way as } v

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the long arrow and then the same arrow divided by 17. The second view is magnified, because an arrow of length 1 would otherwise be hard to see. **Only the length has changed**: the arrow has slid back along its own line until its tip rests on the circle of radius 1.

diagram.alt: A vector (8, 15) of length 17 beside a small circle of radius 1, and then the same vector divided by 17, drawn larger, which ends exactly on the circle of radius 1 and points the same way.
diagram.caption: Dividing by the length slides the arrow back along its own line until it touches the circle of radius 1. The second view is zoomed in so the short arrow is easy to see.

steps.headline: Normalising the vector (5, 12)

lead.text: Normalising takes two moves: find the length, then divide each coordinate by it.

workedSteps.text: Find the length of the vector.
Divide each coordinate by the length.
Check that the result has length 1: its squares must add to 1.

steps.headline: Normalising the vector (3, 4)

lead.text: The length comes first, and one coordinate of the result is left for you.

workedSteps.text: Find the length of the vector.
Divide the first coordinate by the length.

steps.headline: Normalising keeps every sign, and needs a nonzero length

lead.text: Dividing by a length, which is positive, cannot change any sign. The vector (−3, 4) has length 5, so its unit vector is (−0.6, 0.8), with the minus sign exactly where it was, and the explorer shows the two lengths, 5 and then 1, side by side.

The recipe divides by the length, so it needs the length to be *nonzero*. Only the zero vector has length zero, and it points in no direction at all, so it is **the single vector that cannot be normalised**.

steps.headline: Two vectors meet at a right angle exactly when their dot product is zero

lead.text: The [[dot product|Multiply matching coordinates and add the results. Met in 'Dot products and length'.]] of two nonzero vectors is ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ, and the lengths are positive, so the product can be zero only when cos θ is zero, which happens at θ = 90°. Two vectors that meet at a right angle are called **orthogonal**, from the Greek words for *straight* and *angle*, and a dot product of zero is the test for it.
The explorer's first case is (4, 1) and (−1, 4), whose dot product is 4 × (−1) + 1 × 4 = 0. The second case, (4, 1) and (8, 2), points the same way, and its dot product, 34, is large and positive.

afterFigure.text: This also gives a way to build an orthogonal partner: **swap the two coordinates and change the sign of one**. From (a, b) it produces (−b, a), whose dot product with (a, b) is −ab + ba = 0. The zero vector has a dot product of zero with every vector, so it counts as orthogonal to all of them.

steps.headline: Orthogonal vectors of length 1 form an orthonormal pair

lead.text: Orthogonality and length are separate properties, and a pair of vectors can have one without the other. The vectors (5, 0) and (0, −4) are orthogonal, since 5 × 0 + 0 × (−4) = 0, yet they are 5 and 4 long. Two vectors that are orthogonal *and* both of length 1 are called **orthonormal**, as with (1, 0) and (0, 1), or with (0.6, 0.8) and (−0.8, 0.6), whose lengths are √(0.36 + 0.64) = 1 and whose dot product is −0.48 + 0.48 = 0.

Normalising turns any orthogonal pair into an orthonormal one, because it fixes the length without turning either vector. Orthonormal sets are the most convenient axes for a coordinate system, and later lessons build them deliberately and use them to measure how much of one vector lies along another.

lessons.orientation: Recognise perpendicular vectors and turn a nonzero vector into a unit vector.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A vector carries two pieces of information at once, how far it goes and which way, and many questions need only the second. Every direction in the plane corresponds to exactly one point on the circle of radius 1 around the origin, reached by an arrow of length 1, so an arrow of that length records a direction and nothing else, and any nonzero vector can be shrunk or stretched along its own line until it becomes one.

Directions raise a second question, which is whether two of them meet at a right angle. The dot product answers it with a single number, since a right angle turns out to be exactly the case in which that number is zero, and together these two tools give a way of recording and comparing directions using nothing but coordinates.

diagram.caption: Every direction in the plane is one point on the circle of radius 1.

intro.whyItMatters: Unit vectors and right angles are how coordinates record direction, and they return in projections and in every later decomposition.

recap.keyIdea: Dividing by its length turns a nonzero vector into a unit vector, and two vectors are orthogonal exactly when their dot product is zero.

blocks.text: A unit vector keeps the direction of the vector it came from and has length 1, and it exists for every vector except the zero vector. Orthogonal vectors meet at a right angle, which a dot product of zero detects, and a pair that is orthogonal and made of unit vectors is orthonormal.

recap.nextHook: Next, the same numbers are arranged in rows and columns, which gives a matrix, and the first thing to learn is how to read its shape.

lessons.title: Matrix shape and transpose

steps.headline: A matrix is a table of numbers, and its shape is its rows by its columns

lead.text: A **matrix** is a rectangular table of numbers written between brackets. In the figure the table has three lines running across, called **rows**, and two lines running down, called **columns**, and its labels say that each row belongs to a shop and each column to an item, so that *every* number is one shop's price for one item. The three views mark a row, a column, and the table as a whole.

Counting the rows first and then the columns gives the matrix's **shape**, so this table is a 3 × 2 matrix, said "three by two". The order is fixed, and reading it the wrong way round is the commonest slip in the subject.

afterFigure.text: The vectors of earlier lessons are the simplest matrices. A list of three numbers written down the page, $\begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 8 \\ 5\end{pmatrix}$, is a 3 × 1 matrix, called a **column vector**, and from now on a vector is written this way whenever a matrix is about to act on it.

diagram.alt: A table of prices with three rows, one for each shop, and two columns, one for each item. One view marks row 1, one marks column 2, and one marks that the table has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its shape is 3 × 2.
diagram.caption: The price table. Rows run across and columns run down. The shape counts the rows first and then the columns.

steps.headline: An entry is found by its row number and then its column number

lead.text: Each number in a matrix is called an **entry**, and it is named by its position, with the row number first and the column number second, *both* counted from 1. In the price table, the entry in row 3 and column 1 is 9, and the figure marks it together with two others.

afterFigure.text: Entry (1, 2) is 8 while entry (2, 1) is 5, so the two addresses name different places and the order of the pair matters, just as the order of the coordinates mattered for a vector. **The first number of an address is always the row.**

steps.headline: The transpose turns every row into a column

lead.text: Flipping a timetable so that the days run down the side instead of across the top is an operation on tables that has a name. For a matrix it is called the **transpose**, and it is written with a small T. If A = $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 9 & 4 \\ 7 & 1 & 6\end{pmatrix}$, then Aᵀ has as its first column the first row of A, which is (2, 9, 4), and as its second column the second row, (7, 1, 6). The explorer shows A and then Aᵀ, each next to its own transpose.

afterFigure.text: A 2 × 3 matrix becomes a 3 × 2 matrix, because the rows and columns have exchanged roles, and every entry moves with them: **entry (i, j) of Aᵀ is entry (j, i) of A**. The entries themselves do not change, *only* their addresses.

steps.headline: The transpose of a 2 × 3 matrix

lead.text: Take $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 7\end{pmatrix}$, which has 2 rows and 3 columns. Each row of M becomes a column of Mᵀ, one at a time.

workedSteps.text: The first row of M is the first column of the transpose.
The second row of M is the second column.
Putting the two columns side by side gives a matrix with 3 rows and 2 columns.

steps.headline: An entry of the transpose

lead.text: Let A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. The question is the entry in row 3 and column 2 of Aᵀ, and the first two lines show how to locate it.

workedSteps.text: Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ sits in row 3 and column 2 of the transpose, and the transpose swaps the two numbers of an address.
Entry (2, 3) of A is in row 2 and column 3 of A. Read it off.

steps.headline: A matrix acts on a vector only when the shape fits

lead.text: Matrices exist to act on vectors, and the shape says which vectors they can act on. A matrix acts on a column vector by taking the [[dot product|Multiply matching coordinates and add the results. Met in 'Dot products and length'.]] of each of its rows with the vector, and the answers, one per row, make up the result. For A = $\begin{pmatrix}3 & 8 \\ 5 & 1 \\ 9 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and the vector with entries 1 and 0, the three rows give 3 × 1 + 8 × 0 = 3, 5 × 1 + 1 × 0 = 5 and 9 × 1 + 4 × 0 = 9, so the result, written Av, is the column $\begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 5 \\ 9\end{pmatrix}$.

afterFigure.text: A dot product needs two lists of the *same* length, so **a row of A and the vector must have the same number of entries**. A row has one entry for each column of A, and the result has one entry for each row, so a 3 × 2 matrix accepts a vector with 2 entries and returns one with 3. The vector (1, 0) happened to pick out the first column of A, a fact that the next lesson turns into a way of seeing what a matrix does.

lessons.orientation: Read rows and columns, transpose entries and check input dimensions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers, and a timetable with 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side has the same layout: each line running down holds one day, each line running across holds one period, and an entry's position says which day and which period it belongs to. Counting the lines in each direction gives the table's shape, and writing the same entries with the days down the side instead gives a different table, because the two directions carry different meanings.

That second table is called the transpose of the first, and its shape is that of the original with the two numbers exchanged. Reading a shape and exchanging it are the bookkeeping that later calculations depend on, because a matrix acts on a vector by pairing each of its rows with the vector's entries, and that pairing works only when the counts agree.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the shape of a matrix, find any entry from its row and column, and write its transpose.
intro.whyItMatters: A matrix can act only on a vector of the right size, and its shape tells you which sizes fit.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix is a table whose shape is rows by columns, and its transpose turns every row into a column.

blocks.text: An entry is named by its row and then its column, and the transpose moves entry (i, j) to position (j, i), so that a 2 × 3 matrix becomes a 3 × 2 one. A matrix acts on a column vector with as many entries as it has columns, by taking the dot product of each row with the vector.

recap.nextHook: Next, that action is read as a transformation of the plane, which stretches, turns or flattens every vector at once.

lessons.title: Linear transformations

steps.headline: A transformation turns each input vector into an output vector

lead.text: A **transformation**, also called a **map**, is a rule that takes a vector as its input and gives a vector as its output. Many such rules can be written as a formula for each output coordinate in terms of the two input coordinates. The rule that sends (x, y) to (3x + y, x + 2y) sends (1, 1) to (3 + 1, 1 + 2) = (4, 3), and it sends (2, 0) to (6, 2), and the explorer draws each input beside its output.

afterFigure.text: Each input has *exactly* one output, which is found by following the rule, so a transformation behaves like any other function. What makes the transformations of this course special is that a small table of numbers, a matrix, is enough to describe them, as the next screen shows.

steps.headline: The coefficients of the rule are the rows of a matrix

lead.text: Look again at the rule that sends (x, y) to (3x + y, x + 2y). The first output uses the coefficients 3 and 1, and the second uses 1 and 2, so *each* output is the dot product of a row of coefficients with the input. Gathering the rows into a matrix writes the whole rule at once:

afterFigure.text: This is the way of applying a matrix met in the last lesson, taking the [[dot product|Multiply matching coordinates and add the results. Met in 'Dot products and length'.]] of each row with the vector. **The first row of the matrix produces the first output and the second row produces the second**, so a matrix is applied one row at a time.

steps.headline: A matrix map preserves sums and scalar multiples

lead.text: Two facts hold for *every* map that a matrix defines. With the matrix above, (1, 1) goes to (4, 3) and (2, 0) goes to (6, 2), and the two outputs add to (10, 5). The inputs add to (3, 1), and the matrix sends (3, 1) to (3 × 3 + 1, 3 + 2 × 1) = (10, 5), the same vector. Adding first and mapping second gives the same result as mapping first and adding second. Scaling behaves in the same way: tripling the input (1, 1) to (3, 3) gives the output (12, 9), which is three times (4, 3).
In symbols, writing T for the map, u and v for any two vectors and c for any number:

afterFigure.text: A map that obeys both laws is called **linear**, and the name describes the geometry: a linear map sends straight lines to straight lines and keeps evenly spaced points evenly spaced, so a grid of squares comes out as a grid of parallelograms. The number c in the second law may be any [[scalar|A single number with no direction attached. Met in 'Read a vector'.]].

steps.headline: A linear map always sends the zero vector to the zero vector

lead.text: The scaling law has a consequence worth noticing. The zero vector is 0 times any vector v, so T(0) = T(0v) = 0 T(v), and zero times any vector is the zero vector. **Every linear map therefore leaves the origin where it is**, which is why the corner of the square at the origin did not move in the opening figure.

afterFigure.text: The fact gives a quick way to rule maps out. A rule that adds the fixed vector (2, −3) to *every* input slides the whole plane, and it sends the zero vector to (2, −3), so it cannot be linear however simple it looks. A slide of this kind is called a **translation**, and it is the standard example of a transformation that is not linear.

steps.headline: The two columns of a matrix are where (1, 0) and (0, 1) go

lead.text: Every vector can be built from two special ones, e₁ = (1, 0) and e₂ = (0, 1), because (x, y) = x e₁ + y e₂. A linear map respects sums and scalar multiples, so T(x, y) = x T(e₁) + y T(e₂), and *two* outputs are enough to give the output for every input. **Those two outputs are the columns of the map's matrix**, since applying a matrix to (1, 0) picks out its first column and applying it to (0, 1) picks out its second.

A map that turns the plane a quarter turn anticlockwise shows how this works. It sends (1, 0) to (0, 1) and (0, 1) to (−1, 0), so its matrix has those two columns, and it sends (2, 3) to 2(0, 1) + 3(−1, 0) = (−3, 2). The explorer applies the matrix to the three inputs.

afterFigure.text: The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. The rule that took (2, 3) to (−3, 2), swapping the coordinates and changing one sign, is the same rule that built a perpendicular partner for a vector in an earlier lesson, which is what a quarter turn does.

steps.headline: Applying a matrix to (1, 0)

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}4 & -1 \\ 2 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ and apply it to (1, 0), one row at a time.

workedSteps.text: Dot the first row, (4, −1), with (1, 0).
Dot the second row, (2, 6), with (1, 0).
The output is the first column of A.

steps.headline: Applying a matrix to (1, 0), second row

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and apply it to (1, 0). The first row is done, and the second is yours.

workedSteps.text: Dot the first row, (1, −2), with (1, 0).
Dot the second row, (3, 1), with (1, 0) to find the second coordinate of the output.

lessons.orientation: Apply a matrix and distinguish linear maps from translations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Apply the same matrix to every point of the unit square, whose corners are (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 1), and the square comes out as a parallelogram. Its edges stay straight, opposite edges stay parallel, and the corner at the origin stays exactly where it was, so a whole grid of squares drawn on the plane would come out as a grid of parallelograms.

Motions of this kind are called linear maps, and they need very little information to describe: if you know where just two vectors are sent, (1, 0) and (0, 1), you know where every vector goes, and those two destinations can be written as the columns of a small table, a matrix, which can then be applied to any vector.

intro.promise: By the end you'll apply a matrix to a vector, recognise a linear map, and read a map's matrix from where it sends (1, 0) and (0, 1).
intro.whyItMatters: Every matrix is a transformation of the plane, and reading it that way is what the rest of the course relies on.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix is a linear transformation, whose columns are the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1), and a translation is not linear.

blocks.text: Applying a matrix takes the dot product of each row with the input, and the maps it defines preserve sums and scalar multiples, which is what linear means. They always fix the zero vector, so a translation is not linear, and each column of the matrix records where one of the vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) is sent.

recap.nextHook: Next, two maps made one after the other combine into a single map, and its matrix is the product of the two.

lessons.title: Compose matrix maps

steps.headline: Applying one matrix after another is applying a single matrix, their product

lead.text: Take B = $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, which doubles the across-coordinate, and A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, which slides each point across by its height. Starting from (1, 1), B gives (2, 1) and A then gives (3, 1). Carrying out one map after another is called **composing** them, and the composed map is again linear, so it has a matrix of its own. That matrix is the **product** AB, and it is defined by the requirement that (AB)v = A(Bv) for *every* vector v.

To find it, use the fact that a matrix's columns are the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1). B sends (1, 0) to (2, 0), which A leaves at (2, 0), and B sends (0, 1) to (0, 1), which A sends to (1, 1). So the columns of AB are (2, 0) and (1, 1):

afterFigure.text: As a check, AB applied to (1, 1) gives (2 + 1, 1) = (3, 1), which agrees with doing B and then A. **Each column of AB is A applied to a column of B**, and that is the whole idea of matrix multiplication; the next screens turn it into a rule that can be carried out entry by entry.

steps.headline: In AB, the matrix B acts first

lead.text: The matrix written next to the vector acts on it first, so (AB)v means A(Bv) and **B is applied before A**. This is the reverse of the order in which the letters are read, and it matches the way functions are written, since f(g(x)) applies g first. The explorer shows the product for the same two matrices in both orders: AB, with B acting first, and BA, with A acting first.

afterFigure.text: The two results are different matrices, AB with columns (2, 0) and (1, 1) and BA with columns (2, 0) and (2, 1), and they correspond to the two parallelograms of the opening figure. Matrix multiplication is therefore *not commutative*: in general AB and BA differ, even when both exist, which makes it the first habit from ordinary arithmetic that has to be unlearned.

steps.headline: Each entry of a product is a row of A dotted with a column of B

lead.text: Column j of AB is A applied to column j of B, and applying A means taking the dot product of each of its rows with that column. Entry (i, j) of AB, in row i and column j, is therefore the [[dot product|Multiply matching coordinates and add the results. Met in 'Dot products and length'.]] of row i of A with column j of B:

lead.latex: (AB)_{ij} = (\text{row } i \text{ of } A) \cdot (\text{column } j \text{ of } B)

lead.text: For the matrices above, entry (1, 1) is (1, 1) · (2, 0) = 2, entry (1, 2) is (1, 1) · (0, 1) = 1, entry (2, 1) is (0, 1) · (2, 0) = 0, and entry (2, 2) is (0, 1) · (0, 1) = 1, which reproduces the product found from the columns.

afterFigure.text: **Rows of the left matrix pair with columns of the right matrix**, in that order, because the left matrix is the one whose rows do the dotting. The rule can look arbitrary when it is met without its reason, but Arthur Cayley, who set out the algebra of matrices in 1858, chose it for *exactly* this purpose: so that the product of two matrices stands for the composition of the maps they represent.

steps.headline: AB and BA for two matrices

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, which swaps the two coordinates of a vector, and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$, which doubles the first coordinate and triples the second. Each entry of a product is a row dotted with a column.

workedSteps.text: For AB, dot each row of A with each column of B.
For BA, the roles are reversed, and each row of B is dotted with each column of A.
The two products have the same entries in different places, so AB and BA are different matrices.

steps.headline: One entry of AB

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. The pairing is set up, and the dot product is yours.

workedSteps.text: Entry (1, 2) of AB pairs row 1 of A with column 2 of B.
Take the dot product of the row and the column.

steps.headline: A product exists only when the inner shapes match

lead.text: A row of A can be dotted with a column of B *only* if the two have the same number of entries. A row of A has one entry for each column of A, and a column of B has one entry for each row of B, so **AB exists only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B**. When it does, the product has one row for each row of A and one column for each column of B.

A 3 × 2 matrix times a 2 × 4 matrix is therefore a 3 × 4 matrix: the two inner numbers agree and disappear, and the outer numbers give the shape. In general (m × n)(n × p) is m × p. A product can exist in one order and not in the other, since the 2 × 4 matrix times the 3 × 2 matrix has inner numbers 4 and 3, which differ.

steps.headline: The transpose of a product reverses the order

lead.text: Transposing a product gives a result that is easy to get wrong:

**The order reverses**, and the shapes show why it has to. If A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2, then AB and its transpose are both 2 × 2, and BᵀAᵀ is a 2 × 3 matrix times a 3 × 2 matrix, which is 2 × 2 as well. The other order, AᵀBᵀ, would be a 3 × 2 matrix times a 2 × 3 matrix, a 3 × 3 matrix, which *cannot* equal a 2 × 2 one.

afterFigure.text: The entries agree for the same reason. Entry (i, j) of (AB)ᵀ is entry (j, i) of AB, which is row j of A dotted with column i of B, and that is also row i of Bᵀ dotted with column j of Aᵀ, which is entry (i, j) of BᵀAᵀ.

lessons.orientation: Multiply compatible matrices and keep the order of composition.

blocks.text: Take a matrix B that doubles every across-coordinate and a matrix A that slides every point across by an amount equal to its height, and apply B and then A to the unit square. The square is first stretched into a rectangle twice as wide and then slid into a parallelogram, and carrying out one map after another in this way is again a linear map.

Because the combined map is linear, some single matrix must stand for it, and finding that matrix from the two originals is what matrix multiplication is for. The rule looks arbitrary at first, but it comes straight from applying one matrix to the columns of the other, and it lets any chain of transformations, in graphics or in physics, be collapsed into a single table of numbers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply two matrices, say which of them acts first, and tell from the shapes whether a product exists.
intro.whyItMatters: Every chain of transformations, in graphics, in physics and in data, is computed as a matrix product.

recap.keyIdea: The product AB is the matrix of doing B and then A, and each of its entries is a row of A dotted with a column of B.

blocks.text: The matrix next to the vector acts first, so AB and BA are in general different, and the product exists only when the columns of A match the rows of B. Its shape is the rows of A by the columns of B, and its transpose is the product of the transposes in the reverse order.

recap.nextHook: Next, the question of undoing a map: the matrix that changes nothing, and the matrix that reverses another.

lessons.title: Identity and inverses

steps.headline: A map is undone by another map, called its inverse

lead.text: The slide sends (x, y) to (x + y, y). To undo it, take the output (x′, y′) and subtract the height from the across-coordinate, because x′ = x + y and y′ = y mean that the original was (x′ − y′, y′). The input (6, 2) goes to (8, 2) under the slide, and the undoing rule takes (8, 2) back to (8 − 2, 2) = (6, 2). The undoing rule is a linear map in its own right, and its matrix has as columns the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1), namely (1, 0) and (−1, 1).
A matrix that undoes another one is called its **inverse**, and the inverse of A is written A⁻¹. For the slide:

afterFigure.text: Whatever A does to a vector, A⁻¹ reverses, so A⁻¹(Av) = v for *every* v. Undoing is not always possible, however, and a later screen shows a matrix with no inverse at all.

steps.headline: A matrix and its inverse together do nothing, which is the identity matrix

lead.text: Follow a map by its inverse and the result changes no vector at all. The explorer multiplies the slide A by A⁻¹, and then A⁻¹ by A, and both products are the same matrix, which has ones down the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It is called the **identity matrix**:

afterFigure.text: The identity plays the part in matrix multiplication that the number 1 plays in ordinary multiplication, since multiplying by it leaves every vector and every matrix as it was. The inverse can now be defined *exactly*: **A⁻¹ is the matrix for which A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I**. Because AB and BA usually differ, it is worth noticing that a matrix and its inverse give the same result in both orders.

steps.headline: Scalings and slides are undone by reciprocals and by opposite slides

lead.text: Two kinds of map are undone at a glance. A map that scales the across-coordinate by 2 and the up-coordinate by 3 is undone by scaling by ½ and ⅓, so its inverse has **the reciprocals of the scale factors** on its diagonal. A slide that adds three times the height to the across-coordinate is undone by subtracting three times the height, so the 3 in the matrix becomes −3 in the inverse. The explorer shows both inverses.

afterFigure.text: These two cases cover many of the matrices that arise by hand. They also contain a warning: a scale factor of zero could *never* be undone, because zero has no reciprocal, which is the first sign that some matrices have no inverse.

steps.headline: A 2 × 2 matrix has an inverse given by a short formula

lead.text: For a general 2 × 2 matrix A with rows (a, b) and (c, d), the inverse can be written down directly:

The recipe is to swap the two diagonal entries, a and d, to change the signs of the other two, b and c, and to divide *every* entry by the number ad − bc, which is called the **determinant** of A. Multiplying A by the swapped matrix gives ad − bc in both diagonal places and zeros elsewhere, so dividing by ad − bc turns that product into I.

afterFigure.text: The division is the one place where the recipe can fail. **When ad − bc is zero there is nothing to divide by, and no inverse exists.** The determinant will come back in a later lesson with a geometric meaning, which explains why zero is the dividing line.

steps.headline: The inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 7 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, with a = 4, b = 7, c = 1 and d = 2.

workedSteps.text: Work out ad − bc first. It must not be zero, because the formula divides by it.
Swap the diagonal entries, 4 and 2, and change the signs of the other two entries, 7 and 1.
Divide by the determinant, which is 1, so nothing changes.
Check one entry of A A⁻¹: the first row of A with the first column of A⁻¹ should give 1.

steps.headline: One entry of an inverse

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. The determinant is done, and one entry of the inverse is left.

workedSteps.text: Work out the determinant.
Entry (2, 2) of the inverse is a, the entry in the top left of A, divided by the determinant.

steps.headline: A matrix that squashes the plane onto a line cannot be undone

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\end{pmatrix}$, for which ad − bc = 1 × 6 − 3 × 2 = 0. Its second column is three times its first, so A sends (3, 0) to (3, 6) and also sends (0, 1) to (3, 6): two different vectors land on the same output. A map that does this cannot be undone, because from the output (3, 6) nothing says which input it came from. In fact *every* output of A lies on the line through (1, 2), so the whole plane is flattened onto that line.

afterFigure.text: A matrix that has an inverse is called **invertible**, and one that has none is called **singular**. For a 2 × 2 matrix the test is the number ad − bc: when it is not zero the matrix is invertible, and when it is zero the matrix is singular. Later lessons meet the same distinction for larger matrices, through rank and the null space.

steps.headline: An inverse recovers the input from the output

lead.text: The purpose of an inverse is to run a map backwards. If Av = w and A is invertible, multiplying both sides by A⁻¹ gives **v = A⁻¹w**. With A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]], whose inverse is [[1, −1], [−1, 2]], the output w = (3, 2) came from v = (1 × 3 − 1 × 2, −1 × 3 + 2 × 2) = (1, 1), and A(1, 1) = (3, 2) confirms it.

Finding v from Av = w is solving an equation, and the inverse is one way to do it. The next lessons give a second method that works for *every* matrix of any size, including the singular ones, and that tells you exactly how many solutions there are.

lessons.orientation: Undo an invertible square map and recognise when an inverse cannot exist.

blocks.text: The matrix with rows (1, 1) and (0, 1) sends the vector (x, y) to (x + y, y), which slides every point across by an amount equal to its height. If the slide delivers the point (5, 2), the input must also have had height 2, because the slide leaves heights alone, and its across-coordinate must have been 5 − 2 = 3, because the slide added the height to it.

The same reasoning works for every output, so a single map should undo the slide for all points at once, and a matrix that does this is called an inverse. Some matrices have one and some do not, depending on whether the map loses information, which it does exactly when it sends different inputs to the same output.

intro.promise: By the end you'll recognise the identity matrix, find the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix, and tell from ad − bc when no inverse exists.
intro.whyItMatters: Undoing a map is how an output is traced back to the input that made it.

recap.keyIdea: An inverse undoes a map, so that A⁻¹A is the identity, and a 2 × 2 matrix has one exactly when ad − bc is not zero.

blocks.text: The identity matrix changes nothing, and the inverse of A is the matrix with A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I, which for a 2 × 2 matrix is obtained by swapping the diagonal, negating the other two entries, and dividing by ad − bc. When that number is zero the matrix flattens the plane onto a line, sends different vectors to the same output, and has no inverse.

recap.nextHook: Next, a method for solving Av = w that does not need an inverse and works for every matrix.

lessons.title: Solve by row reduction

steps.headline: Adding two equations can make an unknown vanish

lead.text: Take x₁ + x₂ = 7 and x₁ − x₂ = 1. The unknown x₂ has opposite signs in the two equations, so adding them removes it: (x₁ + x₂) + (x₁ − x₂) = 7 + 1 leaves 2x₁ = 8, and x₁ = 4. Putting that into the first equation gives 4 + x₂ = 7, so x₂ = 3, and both original equations hold, since 4 − 3 = 1.

afterFigure.text: Adding is allowed because **equals added to equals are equal**. Each equation says that its two sides are the *same* quantity, so adding the left sides and adding the right sides gives another true equation. The addition has turned a problem with two unknowns into one with a single unknown. The explorer shows this system and a second one, with 2x₂ and −2x₂, which the same addition solves in one step.

steps.headline: A multiple of one equation can be added to another

lead.text: Adding does not always remove an unknown. In x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ + 3x₂ = 12 no unknown has opposite coefficients, but two copies of the first equation, 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 10, can be subtracted from the second. That leaves x₂ = 2, and then x₁ = 5 − 2 = 3, which satisfies both equations, since 2 × 3 + 3 × 2 = 12.

afterFigure.text: The general step is to **add a multiple of one equation to another**, choosing the multiple so that an unknown cancels. Here the multiple was −2, so the second equation was replaced by itself plus −2 times the first. The pair of equations after the step, x₁ + x₂ = 5 and x₂ = 2, has *exactly* the same solutions as the pair before it, and it is far easier to read.

steps.headline: A system is recorded as an augmented matrix, and the steps become row operations

lead.text: Writing x₁ and x₂ in every line is wasteful, because *only* the coefficients and the right-hand sides change. A system is therefore recorded as a matrix with one row for each equation, one column for each unknown, and a last column, set off by a bar, for the right-hand sides. This is the **augmented matrix** of the system, and for x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ − x₂ = 1 it is:

The step used above, adding a multiple of one equation to another, becomes a **row operation**. There are three, and each leaves the solutions of the system unchanged: swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero number, or add a multiple of one row to another. The notation R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁ reads "replace row 2 by row 2 minus twice row 1".

afterFigure.text: A row operation changes a whole row, including its right-hand entry, because **a row stands for an equation, and both sides of an equation must change together**. Each operation can also be reversed, which is why none of them can gain or lose a solution: a swap undoes itself, scaling by a nonzero number is undone by scaling by its reciprocal, and adding a multiple of a row is undone by subtracting it.

steps.headline: Clear the entries below a pivot, then read the answer from the bottom up

lead.text: To solve a system, take the first nonzero entry of the top row, called its **pivot**, and use row operations to make *every* entry below it zero. For x₁ + x₂ = 6 and 3x₁ + 2x₂ = 14 the pivot is the 1 at the top left, and R₂ ← R₂ − 3R₁ turns the second row into (0, −1 | −4):

The second row now says −x₂ = −4, so x₂ = 4, and the first row then gives x₁ + 4 = 6, so x₁ = 2. Solving from the last row upwards, putting each value found into the rows above it, is called **back-substitution**.

afterFigure.text: The new system is triangular: every row has fewer unknowns than the one above it, which is what makes the bottom-up reading possible. **Row reduction is the procedure of making a system triangular with row operations and then back-substituting.**

steps.headline: Solving x₁ + 2x₂ = 8 and 3x₁ + x₂ = 9

lead.text: Record the system, clear below the pivot, and read the answer from the bottom up.

workedSteps.text: Write the augmented matrix.
Clear below the pivot with R₂ ← R₂ − 3R₁, changing the right-hand entry along with the rest of the row.
The second row says −5x₂ = −15, so divide by −5.
Put x₂ = 3 into the first row, which says x₁ + 2x₂ = 8.
Check the answer in the original second equation.

steps.headline: Swapping rows, then clearing

lead.text: A pivot of 1 is easier to work with than a pivot of 2, so the rows of 2x₁ + 5x₂ = 16 and x₁ + 2x₂ = 7 are swapped first. The last step is yours.

workedSteps.text: Write the augmented matrix with the rows swapped, so that the pivot is 1.
Clear below the pivot with R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁, which gives x₂ = 2.
Put x₂ = 2 into the first row to find x₁.

steps.headline: With more unknowns the same two moves repeat

lead.text: Nothing changes when there are more unknowns: **clear below the first pivot, then below the second, and so on**, until the system is triangular, and then back-substitute. Take the triangular system x₁ + 2x₂ + x₃ = 9, x₂ − x₃ = 1 and 2x₃ = 6. The last equation gives x₃ = 3, the middle one gives x₂ − 3 = 1, so x₂ = 4, and the first gives x₁ + 8 + 3 = 9, so x₁ = −2.

afterFigure.text: Each extra unknown adds one more clearing step and one more substitution, so the work grows steadily with the size of the system, which is why computers solve very large systems this way. The procedure is called Gaussian elimination, after Carl Friedrich Gauss, although the Chinese text *The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art* describes the same elimination on arrays of numbers many centuries earlier.

lessons.orientation: Use equivalent row operations to solve A x = b and check the result.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two equations in two unknowns, such as x₁ + x₂ = 7 and x₁ − x₂ = 1, can be pictured as two straight lines, and a pair of numbers satisfies both equations exactly when it is a point on both lines. These two lines cross at a single point, and the coordinates of that point are the answer.

Reading an answer from a graph is slow and inexact, and it fails altogether with three or more unknowns, where the picture can no longer be drawn. A short list of exact steps does the work instead, by rewriting the system as one with the same solutions whose answer can be read off, and unlike the inverse of the previous lesson, the steps work whether or not the matrix has an inverse.

intro.promise: By the end you'll solve a system of equations with row operations and check the answer by substituting it back.
intro.whyItMatters: Row reduction is the standard way to solve linear systems, and it is the tool the next lessons use to count solutions.

recap.keyIdea: A system is solved by row operations that clear the entries below each pivot, followed by back-substitution.

blocks.text: Each equation is a row of the augmented matrix, and swapping rows, scaling a row by a nonzero number, or adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the solutions unchanged. Using them to make the system triangular, and then reading the unknowns from the last row upwards, solves it, and the answer can always be checked in the original equations.

recap.nextHook: Next, the same procedure shows when a system has exactly one solution, when it has none, and when it has infinitely many.

lessons.title: One, none or many solutions

steps.headline: A row that reads 0 = c, with c not zero, means there is no solution

lead.text: Row operations can produce a row whose coefficients are all zero. Take x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 12. The operation R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁ turns the second row into (0, 0 | 2):

That row says 0x₁ + 0x₂ = 2, which is 0 = 2, and no values of x₁ and x₂ can make it true, since the left side is zero whatever they are. A solution has to satisfy *every* row, so the system has none. A system with no solution is called **inconsistent**, and one with at least one solution is **consistent**.

afterFigure.text: The picture is two parallel lines. The second equation says 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 12, which is x₁ + x₂ = 6, and that line runs beside x₁ + x₂ = 5 without ever meeting it. **The sign to look for is a row of zeros on the left with a nonzero number on the right.**

steps.headline: A row that reads 0 = 0 leaves an unknown free to take any value

lead.text: Change the right side of the second equation in that system from 12 to 10, so that x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 10. The same operation now gives (0, 0 | 0), a row that says 0 = 0 and is always true. The second equation was just double the first, so it added no restriction, and what is left is the single equation x₁ + x₂ = 5 in two unknowns.

Any value can be chosen for x₁, and x₂ = 5 − x₁ then follows, so (0, 5), (1, 4), (2, 3) and a boundless supply of further pairs are all solutions. In the reduced matrix *only* the first column has a pivot. The unknown belonging to a column without a pivot is called a **free variable**, because it can take any value, and the unknowns at the pivots are then fixed by it. The explorer sets this system beside the inconsistent one.

steps.headline: x₁ + x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 6

lead.text: The second equation looks like twice the first. Reduce the system and read what is left.

workedSteps.text: Clear below the pivot with R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁.
The second row reads 0 = 0 and gives no restriction, and the second column has no pivot, so x₂ is free. Decide how many solutions the system has.

steps.headline: A pivot in every unknown's column means exactly one solution

lead.text: Whether a consistent system has one solution or many depends on its pivots. In the reduced system (1, 0 | 4) and (0, 1 | 1), both columns have a pivot, so the rows say x₁ = 4 and x₂ = 1, and there is exactly one solution. In (1, 2 | 4) and (0, 0 | 0) *only* the first column has a pivot, so x₂ is free and x₁ = 4 − 2x₂, which gives a different solution for every choice of x₂. The explorer shows both.

afterFigure.text: The three possible outcomes can now be read from the reduced system. **If a row reads 0 = c with c not zero, there is no solution. Otherwise there is exactly one solution when every unknown has a pivot, and infinitely many when some unknown is free.** No linear system has exactly two solutions, or any other number greater than one, because two solutions would put every point of the line through them among the solutions as well.

steps.headline: Classifying x₁ + 2x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 4x₂ = 7

lead.text: Reduce the system, and then read the last row before looking for anything else.

workedSteps.text: Write the augmented matrix.
Clear below the pivot with R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁. The right-hand entry becomes 7 − 2 × 3 = 1.
The second row reads 0 = 1.
The system is inconsistent, with no solution, and nothing further needs to be done.

steps.headline: A consistent system has as many free variables as unknowns minus pivots

lead.text: Every unknown either has a pivot or is free, so in a consistent system **the number of free variables is the number of unknowns less the number of pivots**. Take x₁ + 2x₂ + x₃ = 6 and x₃ = 2. There are three unknowns, and the pivots are in the first and third columns, so there is *one* free variable, x₂. Setting x₂ = t gives x₃ = 2 and x₁ = 6 − 2t − 2 = 4 − 2t, so (4 − 2t, t, 2) is a solution for every t, and t = 0 gives (4, 0, 2), where 4 + 0 + 2 = 6.

afterFigure.text: Each free variable is a degree of freedom in the solution set. One free variable gives a line of solutions, as here, two give a plane, and so on, and four unknowns with two pivots would leave two free. The count of pivots, which fixes the count of free variables, is the quantity a later lesson calls the rank.

steps.headline: A system with zeros on the right always has the zero solution

lead.text: A system whose right-hand sides are all zero, written Ax = 0, is called **homogeneous**. Putting every unknown equal to zero makes every left side zero, so the zero vector always solves it, and it is called the *trivial solution*. A homogeneous system is therefore never inconsistent: the row 0 = c with c not zero cannot appear, because row operations on a column of zeros leave it zero.

Only two outcomes remain. If every unknown has a pivot, the trivial solution is the only one. If some unknown is free, there are infinitely many solutions, such as (t, t) for the single equation x₁ − x₂ = 0, whose second unknown is free. Homogeneous systems return in the lesson on rank and the null space, where their solutions form an important set of their own.

lessons.orientation: Classify systems using contradictions, pivots and free variables.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A system of two equations in two unknowns asks where two straight lines meet, and two lines in a plane can do one of three things. They can cross at a single point, they can run side by side and never meet, or they can lie exactly on top of each other and share every point. In the first case the system has one solution, in the second none, and in the third infinitely many.

No other outcome is possible for a linear system, however many unknowns it has, although a system with more unknowns cannot be drawn so simply. Which of the three applies can be read from the reduced rows without drawing anything, so it is known before any solution has been searched for.

diagram.alt: Three grids, each with two straight lines. In the first the lines cross at one point. In the second they run side by side and never meet. In the third one line lies exactly on top of the other.
diagram.caption: Two lines in a plane can cross, run side by side, or coincide. Each case is a different kind of system.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell from the reduced rows whether a system has one solution, none or infinitely many, and count its free variables.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing the number of solutions before searching for them is what makes row reduction a complete method.

recap.keyIdea: A reduced row 0 = c with c not zero means no solution; otherwise a free variable means infinitely many and none means exactly one.

blocks.text: Reducing a system exposes its type: an inconsistent row means no solution, and for a consistent system the unknowns without pivots are free and number the unknowns less the pivots. A homogeneous system always has the zero solution, so it has either that one or infinitely many.

recap.nextHook: Next, the solutions of a system are described as all the linear combinations of a few vectors, which leads to the idea of a span.

lessons.title: Spans and subspaces

steps.headline: All the multiples of one vector lie on a line through the origin

lead.text: Scale the vector (1, 2) by *every* number c and the results, (c, 2c), are the points of a straight line through the origin: (2, 4), (−1, −2), (0.5, 1) and all the rest. The set of every [[linear combination|Scaled vectors added together. Met in 'Add and scale vectors'.]] of some given vectors is called their **span**, so this line is the span of (1, 2). The explorer draws the span of (1, 2) and the span of (3, 1).

afterFigure.text: A span always contains the zero vector, which is the combination with every coefficient zero. It also cannot be escaped by combining its own members: c(1, 2) + d(1, 2) = (c + d)(1, 2), and a multiple of a multiple is a multiple. **A span is a set that further combining never leaves**, and the second half of the lesson makes that precise.

steps.headline: A second vector adds a direction only if it is not a multiple of the first

lead.text: Add the vector (1, 0) to (1, 2). Every point of the plane can now be reached, because the new vector points in a direction that the first one could *never* produce. With the vectors (2, 1) and (6, 3) the picture is quite different: since (6, 3) = 3(2, 1), every combination c₁(2, 1) + c₂(6, 3) equals (c₁ + 3c₂)(2, 1), a multiple of (2, 1), so the span is still only a line. The explorer shows both pairs.

afterFigure.text: The number of genuinely different directions in a span is called its **dimension**. The span of the zero vector alone is a single point, of dimension 0, a line has dimension 1, and the whole plane has dimension 2. Two vectors in the plane therefore span the whole plane, with dimension 2, unless one of them is a multiple of the other, in which case the dimension is at most 1.

steps.headline: Finding how much of each vector reaches a point means solving a system

lead.text: To reach a given point the coefficients of the combination are the unknowns. To write (6, 2) as c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1), match the coordinates: the first gives c₁ + c₂ = 6 and the second gives c₂ = 2. So c₂ = 2 and c₁ = 4, and the check is 4(1, 0) + 2(1, 1) = (4 + 2, 2) = (6, 2).

afterFigure.text: Matching coordinates always produces a system of linear equations in the coefficients, which is the kind of system that row reduction solves. **The point lies in the span exactly when that system has a solution**, so an inconsistent system means the point *cannot* be reached. Written with the vectors as the columns of a matrix A and the coefficients as the unknowns x, the question is whether Ax = b has a solution.

steps.headline: Writing (8, 5) as c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1)

lead.text: Match the coordinates, and use the coordinate in which only one coefficient appears.

workedSteps.text: Write the equation one coordinate at a time.
The second coordinate gives c₂ on its own.
Put c₂ = 5 into the first coordinate.
Check the combination.

steps.headline: Writing (5, 3) as c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1)

lead.text: The same two vectors again, with a different target. The second coordinate is done, and the first is yours.

workedSteps.text: Match the coordinates, and read c₂ from the second.
Put c₂ = 3 into the first coordinate to find c₁.

steps.headline: A subspace is a set that combining its members cannot leave

lead.text: A set of vectors is a **subspace** of the plane if it passes three tests: it contains the zero vector, the sum of any two of its members is again a member, and any multiple of a member is again a member. The points (x, y) with y = 3x pass all three. The point (0, 0) is on the line, the sum (x, 3x) + (x′, 3x′) = (x + x′, 3(x + x′)) is on the line, and the multiple c(x, 3x) = (cx, 3cx) is on it too.

afterFigure.text: Every span passes the tests for the reason seen earlier, since a combination of combinations is a combination, so **every span is a subspace**. The converse also holds in the plane, where the *only* subspaces are the single point at the origin, the lines through the origin, and the whole plane, of dimensions 0, 1 and 2.

steps.headline: A set that misses the origin cannot be a subspace

lead.text: The first test gives the quickest way to rule a set out. The line y = x − 3 passes through (3, 0) and (0, −3), but it does not contain (0, 0), since 0 is not 0 − 3, so it is not a subspace. Any line that misses the origin fails in the *same* way. It is a line through the origin that has been slid sideways, by the kind of translation met in an earlier lesson, and sliding takes the zero vector off the set.

afterFigure.text: Passing the zero test is necessary but not sufficient. The first quadrant, the points with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, contains zero and is closed under addition, but multiplying (1, 1) by −1 gives (−1, −1), which has left the set, so it fails the third test. **Zero first, then addition and scaling**, is a sound order for checking a set.

lessons.orientation: Describe all linear combinations and test the conditions for a subspace.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two vectors, such as (1, 2) and (1, 0), can be combined by scaling each and adding the results, and c₁(1, 2) + c₂(1, 0) is a new vector for every choice of the two numbers c₁ and c₂. If the numbers are restricted to whole values the combinations form a regular lattice of points, but when they may take any value the gaps close, and every point (x, y) of the plane is reached, with c₁ = y/2 and c₂ = x − y/2.

Any set of vectors raises the question of which points can be reached by combining them, and the answer is always a flat shape through the origin, such as a point, a line or a plane. Knowing which one tells you what the vectors can do together and, when a target lies outside the shape, that no choice of coefficients will reach it.
