intro.promise: By the end you'll describe everything a set of vectors can reach, find the coefficients that reach a given point, and test whether a set is a subspace.
intro.whyItMatters: Spans and subspaces are the language in which every later idea, from solutions of systems to rank, is stated.

recap.keyIdea: The span of some vectors is everything their combinations reach, and it is a subspace: a set containing zero and closed under sums and multiples.

blocks.text: The span of a vector is a line, and two vectors span the plane unless one is a multiple of the other, so the dimension of a span counts its independent directions. A point lies in a span when matching coordinates gives a consistent system for the coefficients, and a set that misses the origin can never be a subspace.

recap.nextHook: Next, the smallest set of vectors that still spans a subspace, a basis, and how its vectors act as coordinates.

lessons.title: Basis and dimension

steps.headline: A vector that is a combination of the others is redundant

lead.text: Remove (3, 4) from the three vectors above and nothing is lost, because any combination that uses it can be rewritten without it: c(3, 4) = c(2, 1) + c(1, 3). A set of vectors in which none can be written as a combination of the others is called **linearly independent**, and a set in which some vector can be is called dependent. The explorer shows the span of all three vectors and then of just the first two, and it is the *same* whole plane both times.

afterFigure.text: There is an equivalent test that is easier to apply. Rewriting (3, 4) = (2, 1) + (1, 3) as 1(2, 1) + 1(1, 3) − 1(3, 4) = (0, 0) gives a combination, with coefficients that are not all zero, that comes to the zero vector. **A set is independent exactly when the only combination that gives zero is the one with every coefficient zero.** For two vectors the test reduces to asking whether one is a multiple of the other.

steps.headline: A basis is a spanning set with nothing redundant

lead.text: A **basis** of a subspace is a set of vectors that spans the subspace and is linearly independent: it reaches everything in the subspace, and it has no vector to spare. The plane has many bases. The vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) form one, and (1, 1) and (1, −1) form another, since neither is a multiple of the other and the two together reach every point of the plane. The explorer shows that both pairs span the whole plane.

afterFigure.text: Every basis of a given subspace has the same number of vectors, and that number is its [[dimension|The number of independent directions in a span. Met in 'Spans and subspaces'.]]. This makes the count of directions from the last lesson exact: a basis of a line has one vector, a basis of the plane has two, and the set containing *only* the zero vector has a basis with none.

steps.headline: A basis gives every vector exactly one recipe, which is its coordinates

lead.text: Take the basis (1, 1) and (1, −1), and write the vector (6, 2) as c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1). Matching coordinates gives c₁ + c₂ = 6 and c₁ − c₂ = 2, and adding the two equations gives 2c₁ = 8, so c₁ = 4 and c₂ = 2. The pair (4, 2) is called the **coordinates** of (6, 2) in this basis. With the standard basis (1, 0) and (0, 1) the coordinates are the ordinary ones, since (6, 2) = 6(1, 0) + 2(0, 1).

afterFigure.text: No other pair of numbers works, because **a basis gives each vector exactly one recipe**. Spanning guarantees that at least one recipe exists. If there were two, subtracting them would give a combination of the basis vectors with coefficients not all zero that comes to zero, which independence forbids. Different bases give the same vector different coordinates, but each basis gives it *only* one set.

steps.headline: The coordinates of (5, 1) in the basis (1, 1), (1, −1)

lead.text: Match the coordinates to get two equations for the two unknown coefficients, and then solve them.

workedSteps.text: Write (5, 1) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1), one coordinate at a time.
Add the two equations, which removes c₂.
Put c₁ = 3 into the first equation.
The coordinates are (3, 2), and they are the only possible ones.

steps.headline: The coordinates of (6, 4) in the same basis

lead.text: The equations are set up, and the first coefficient is yours.

workedSteps.text: Match the coordinates of (6, 4) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1).
Add the two equations and divide, to find c₁.

steps.headline: In the plane, two vectors suffice and three never can

lead.text: The plane has dimension 2, so every basis of it has exactly two vectors. Fewer than two cannot reach every point, and *any* three vectors in the plane are dependent, because one of them can always be built from the other two. It follows that **two vectors in the plane form a basis exactly when they are independent**, which for two vectors means that neither is a multiple of the other. For (3, 1) and (1, 2) that holds, so they span a plane of dimension 2.

The same counting works beyond the plane. The three vectors (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1) form a basis of three-dimensional space, so that space has dimension 3, and any three independent vectors in it do the same job.

steps.headline: The zero vector can never belong to a basis

lead.text: Suppose a set contains the zero vector, as in the pair (2, 3) and (0, 0). Then 0 × (2, 3) + 1 × (0, 0) = (0, 0) is a combination with a coefficient that is not zero, and it comes to the zero vector, so the set is dependent. The zero vector also adds *no* new points to a span, since every multiple of it is again zero. A set that contains it is therefore **never a basis**, and its span is no larger than the span of the other vectors.

lessons.orientation: Find a spanning independent set and use its vectors as coordinates.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The vectors (2, 1), (1, 3) and (3, 4) all lie in the plane, and the first two already reach every point of it, since neither is a multiple of the other. The third adds nothing, because (3, 4) = (2, 1) + (1, 3), which makes it the diagonal of the parallelogram built on the other two, and any combination that uses it can be rewritten without it.

A set containing a vector of that kind carries a redundancy, so the natural description of a subspace is the smallest set of vectors that still reaches everything in it. Such a set gives every vector exactly one recipe, so that its members can serve as the units of a coordinate system, and the number of vectors it needs is the same however the set is chosen.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test whether vectors form a basis, count the dimension of a span, and write a vector in the coordinates of a basis.
intro.whyItMatters: A basis is the standard way to describe a subspace, and changing basis is the idea behind diagonalisation.

recap.keyIdea: A basis is an independent set that spans a subspace, it gives every vector exactly one set of coordinates, and its size is the dimension.

blocks.text: A vector that can be built from the others is redundant, and a basis has none. Every basis of a subspace has the same number of vectors, so the plane has dimension 2, and the coordinates of a vector in a basis are the coefficients of its one recipe, found by solving a system.

recap.nextHook: Next, the pivots of a matrix show how many independent columns it has, and the inputs it sends to zero form a subspace of their own.

lessons.title: Rank and null space

steps.headline: The inputs a matrix sends to zero form a subspace, its null space

lead.text: The set of all vectors x with Ax = 0 is called the **null space** of A. It is the solution set of the homogeneous system met earlier, so it always contains the zero vector. For the matrix with rows (1, 2) and (2, 4), the second row repeats the first, and the equation x₁ + 2x₂ = 0 gives x = (−2t, t), the multiples of (2, −1), which is a line through the origin. The explorer applies the matrix to (2, −1), which vanishes, and to (1, 1), which does not.

afterFigure.text: The null space is a subspace. If Ax = 0 and Ay = 0, then A(x + y) = Ax + Ay = 0 and A(cx) = c Ax = 0, so sums and multiples of its members stay in it, which together with the zero vector gives the three tests of the previous lesson. **The null space records what the matrix throws away**: two inputs that differ by a vector of the null space produce the *same* output.

steps.headline: The outputs of a matrix are the combinations of its columns

lead.text: Multiplying a matrix by a vector can be read in a second way. For B = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and x = (3, 1, 2), the rows give (3 + 0 + 4, 0 + 1 + 6) = (7, 7), and the same result is 3(1, 0) + 1(0, 1) + 2(2, 3), which is x₁ times column 1, plus x₂ times column 2, plus x₃ times column 3. In general Ax is the combination of the columns of A whose coefficients are the entries of x.

afterFigure.text: The set of all possible outputs is therefore the span of the columns, which is called the **column space** of A. For B, the first two columns, (1, 0) and (0, 1), already span the plane, so every vector of the plane is an output. The explorer's second case, x = (0, 0, 4), uses *only* the third column and gives 4(2, 3) = (8, 12), which is one output among them.

steps.headline: The rank counts the pivots, and the pivot columns span the column space

lead.text: Row reduction measures the size of the column space. The number of pivots of a matrix is called its **rank**, and it equals the dimension of the column space. The matrix B above is already reduced, with pivots in columns 1 and 2, so its rank is 2, and the pivot columns (1, 0) and (0, 1) form a basis for its column space. The third column, (2, 3), equals 2(1, 0) + 3(0, 1), so it brings nothing new.

afterFigure.text: In general the pivot columns are independent and every other column is a combination of them, which is why the number of pivots counts the independent directions among the columns. A matrix with a pivot in every row, as B has, reaches every vector of the output space, and a smaller rank means that some directions of the output are *never* reached.

steps.headline: The nullity counts the free columns, and rank plus nullity is the number of columns

lead.text: The unknowns of Bx = 0 that have no pivot are free, and each contributes one direction to the null space. Column 3 of B has no pivot, so x₃ = t is free, and the rows give x₁ = −2t and x₂ = −3t. The null space is the line of multiples of (−2, −3, 1), and B(−2, −3, 1) = (−2 + 0 + 2, 0 − 3 + 3) = (0, 0) confirms it. The dimension of the null space is called the **nullity**, so B has nullity 1.

afterFigure.text: Every column either has a pivot and counts towards the rank, or is free and counts towards the nullity, so **rank + nullity = the number of columns**. For B that is 2 + 1 = 3. This is the rank–nullity theorem, and it says that what a matrix keeps and what it throws away together account for *every* direction of the input.

steps.headline: Rank, nullity and a column-space basis for a 2 × 3 matrix

lead.text: Take E = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 7\end{pmatrix}$. Reduce it first, and then read each quantity from the pivots.

workedSteps.text: Clear below the pivot with R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁.
The pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so the rank is 2.
The nullity is the number of columns minus the rank.
The free column is column 2. Setting x₂ = t gives x₃ = 0 and x₁ = −2t, so the null space is the multiples of (−2, 1, 0).
A basis for the column space is the pivot columns of E itself, columns 1 and 3.

steps.headline: The rank of a reduced matrix

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, which is already reduced. The pivots are marked, and counting them is yours.

workedSteps.text: Row 1 starts with a 1 in column 1, and row 2 has its first nonzero entry, a 1, in column 3.
Count the pivots to find the rank.

steps.headline: A basis for the column space comes from the columns of the original matrix

lead.text: Row reduction finds *which* columns are pivot columns, but **the basis vectors themselves must be taken from the original matrix**. For the matrix with rows (1, 0, 3) and (0, 2, 4), the pivot columns are 1 and 2, so (1, 0) and (0, 2) are a basis for the column space, while column 3, (3, 4), equals 3(1, 0) + 2(0, 2) and adds nothing.

The reduced matrix cannot be used for the vectors, because row operations change the column space. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has only multiples of (1, 1) as outputs, but its reduced form $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ has only multiples of (1, 0). The positions of the pivots survive the row operations, and that is all that is taken from the reduction.

lessons.orientation: Connect pivot columns, column space and the inputs a matrix sends to zero.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The matrix with rows (1, 2) and (2, 4) sends the vector (2, −1) to (0, 0), because 1 × 2 + 2 × (−1) = 0 and 2 × 2 + 4 × (−1) = 0. A nonzero vector has been carried to zero, and so has every multiple of it, which means that a whole line of inputs collapses to the origin. The outputs cannot go everywhere either: every output of this matrix is a multiple of (1, 2), since it sends (x, y) to (x + 2y)(1, 2), so they too lie on a single line.

Two subspaces therefore describe what a matrix does: the inputs it sends to zero and the outputs it can produce. Their sizes are tied together by a short, exact rule, and finding them comes down to counting the pivots met in the previous lessons.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the rank and nullity of a matrix from its pivots, test whether a vector is sent to zero, and pick a basis for the outputs.
intro.whyItMatters: Rank and null space say how much of the input a matrix keeps and how much it destroys, and every later decomposition builds on that split.

recap.keyIdea: The rank is the number of pivots and the dimension of the column space, the nullity counts the free columns, and together they make up the number of columns.

blocks.text: The column space is everything the matrix can produce and the null space is everything it sends to zero, and both are subspaces. A basis for the column space is the set of pivot columns of the original matrix, and the pivot positions fix the nullity as the number of columns less the rank.

recap.nextHook: Next, a single number, the determinant, measures how a square matrix scales area, and it is zero exactly when the matrix collapses the plane.

lessons.title: Determinants and volume

steps.headline: A matrix multiplies every area by the same factor

lead.text: The simplest matrices stretch each axis on its own. The matrix with rows (3, 0) and (0, 4) multiplies across-distances by 3 and up-distances by 4, so a unit square becomes a rectangle with sides 3 and 4, and area 12. Because the map is linear, a grid of unit squares goes to a grid of identical rectangles, so *every* region has its area multiplied by 12. The number by which a matrix multiplies area is called its **area factor**. The explorer shows this stretch and a second one, by 2 in both directions, whose area factor is 4.

afterFigure.text: For a stretch of this kind the area factor is the product of the diagonal entries. The [[determinant|The number ad − bc of a 2 × 2 matrix. Met in 'Identity and inverses'.]], ad − bc, equals ad here, because the other diagonal is zero. The next screens show that the determinant is the area factor for every 2 × 2 matrix, and that its sign and its zero value also mean something.

steps.headline: The determinant ad − bc is the area of the parallelogram the columns span

lead.text: A matrix that is not diagonal turns the unit square into a leaning parallelogram, whose sides are the columns of the matrix. For the matrix with rows (3, 1) and (2, 2) the sides are the columns (3, 2) and (1, 2), and the parallelogram they span has area 4, which is the determinant 3 × 2 − 1 × 2. In general the parallelogram with sides (a, c) and (b, d) has area |ad − bc|, so the determinant gives the area factor of any 2 × 2 matrix, up to a sign that a later screen explains. The explorer shows this matrix beside the stretch with rows (3, 0) and (0, 2).

afterFigure.text: One way to see why a lean costs nothing is to slide it. The matrix with rows (1, 1) and (0, 1), which moves each point across by its height, has determinant 1 × 1 − 1 × 0 = 1 and turns a square into a parallelogram with the *same* base and the same height, hence the same area. **A shear changes the shape of a region and leaves its area alone.**

steps.headline: A negative determinant reverses orientation, and a zero determinant means collapse

lead.text: The determinant can be negative or zero, and both carry meaning. The matrix with rows (0, 1) and (1, 0) swaps the two coordinates, and its determinant is 0 × 0 − 1 × 1 = −1. It reflects the plane in the diagonal line, so areas are unchanged, but the picture is turned into its mirror image: the turn from the first column to the second, which ran anticlockwise before, runs clockwise afterwards. A negative determinant records this reversal of **orientation**, and the area factor is its absolute value. Swapping two rows of a matrix has the *same* effect, and changes the sign of its determinant.

A determinant of zero means an area factor of zero. The matrix with rows (2, 4) and (1, 2) has the columns (2, 1) and (4, 2), the second being twice the first, so its determinant is 2 × 2 − 4 × 1 = 0, and it flattens the whole plane onto the line through (2, 1). This is the collapse met in the lesson on inverses, and its test now has a reason: **a square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not zero**, since a map that squashes the plane onto a line cannot be undone.

steps.headline: The determinant of the matrix with rows (1, 4) and (3, 5)

lead.text: Compute the two diagonal products separately, then subtract, and read what the answer says about area and orientation.

workedSteps.text: Multiply along the main diagonal.
Multiply along the other diagonal.
Subtract the second product from the first.
The area factor is the size of the determinant, and the minus sign says that orientation is reversed.

steps.headline: The determinant of the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 3)

lead.text: The two diagonal products are worked out, and the subtraction is yours.

workedSteps.text: Multiply along the main diagonal.
Multiply along the other diagonal.
Subtract to find the determinant.

lead.text: These are the rows of the previous matrix in the opposite order.

steps.headline: The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants

lead.text: When one map follows another, the area factors *multiply*: a map that doubles area followed by one that triples it multiplies area by 6. In matrix terms, **det(AB) = det(A) × det(B)**. Take A with rows (2, 0) and (0, 1), whose determinant is 2, and B with rows (1, 1) and (0, 3), whose determinant is 3. Their product has rows (2, 2) and (0, 3), and its determinant is 2 × 3 − 2 × 0 = 6, which is 2 × 3.

Two consequences follow. A matrix and its inverse multiply to the identity, whose determinant is 1, so the inverse has determinant 1/det(A), and a singular matrix, with determinant 0, makes every product containing it singular as well. Determinants were found before matrices were: Seki Takakazu in Japan and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in Europe both arrived at them in the later seventeenth century, while looking for a test that tells when a system of equations can be solved.

steps.headline: In three dimensions the determinant is a volume factor

lead.text: A 3 × 3 matrix carries the unit cube to a box with slanted faces, called a parallelepiped, whose edges are the three columns, and its determinant is **the signed factor by which the matrix multiplies volume**. For a matrix that stretches the three axes separately the factor is the product of the three diagonal entries: scales of 2, 5 and 3 turn a cube of volume 1 into a box with edges 2, 5 and 3, and volume 30.

The signs and the zero work as they did in the plane. A negative determinant reverses orientation, as a mirror does, and a determinant of zero means that the box has been *flattened* into a plane, a line or a point, so the matrix cannot be undone. The determinant of a product is still the product of the determinants.

lessons.orientation: Read signed area and volume factors and use zero determinant to detect collapse.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A matrix carries the unit square, whose area is 1, to a parallelogram whose sides are the images of the square's sides, and for the matrix with columns (2, 1) and (1, 2) that parallelogram has area 3. A linear map treats every region alike, turning a grid of unit squares into a grid of equal parallelograms, so the area of every region is multiplied by the same number, here 3.

A single number, readable from the entries of the matrix, therefore says how much the map stretches or shrinks area. Its sign says whether the map has turned the plane over like a mirror, and when it is zero the map has squashed the plane flat, which is the failure of inverses seen in an earlier lesson.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute a 2 × 2 determinant, read it as a signed area factor, and use a zero determinant to detect a matrix with no inverse.
intro.whyItMatters: The determinant gives one number that says whether a square matrix can be undone, and by how much it scales space.

recap.keyIdea: The determinant of a square matrix is its signed area, or volume, factor: its size is the scaling, its sign records a flip, and zero means the map collapses.

blocks.text: For a 2 × 2 matrix the determinant ad − bc is the area of the parallelogram the columns span, with a minus sign when orientation is reversed, and it is 0 when the columns lie on one line. Area factors multiply under composition, so det(AB) = det(A) det(B), and a matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not zero.

recap.nextHook: Next, the dot product and the idea of the closest point combine to project a vector onto a line.

lessons.title: Project onto a direction

steps.headline: The projection of a vector onto a line is the point of the line nearest to it

lead.text: The easiest line to start with is the across axis. A point at (8, 3) dropped straight down onto it lands at (8, 0), keeping its across distance and losing its height. The point (8, 0) is the point of the axis nearest to (8, 3), and it is called the **projection** of the vector (8, 3) onto that line. The line is described by a direction d, and the explorer uses d = (1, 0) and then d = (2, 0), which point along the same line and give the same projection.

afterFigure.text: What is left over, the vector from the projection to the original point, is called the **residual**: here it is (8, 3) − (8, 0) = (0, 3), pointing straight up at a right angle to the line. **The projection depends only on the line, and not on the length or the sign of the direction chosen to describe it**, because *every* direction vector of the line spans the same set.

steps.headline: On a slanted line the projection is a multiple of the direction

lead.text: A slanted line needs a calculation. Take the vector v = (0, 5) and the line spanned by d = (1, 2). The projection is some multiple c d of the direction, and the residual v − c d must meet the line at a right angle, which means that its dot product with d is zero: (v − c d) · d = 0. Expanding this gives v · d = c (d · d), so the multiple is c = (v · d)/(d · d). Here v · d = 10 and d · d = 5, so c = 2 and the projection is (2, 4). The explorer shows it, and shows that the direction (2, 4) gives the *same* point.

afterFigure.text: The residual is (0, 5) − (2, 4) = (−2, 1), and its dot product with d is −2 + 2 = 0, which confirms the right angle. **The coefficient c is a ratio of two dot products**, the one that measures how far v extends along d divided by the one that measures the length of d squared.

steps.headline: Dot, divide and scale: three steps give any projection

lead.text: The recipe has three steps. **Take the dot product of v with d, divide by the dot product of d with itself, and scale d by the result**:

The recipe simplifies when d is a unit vector, because d · d is then 1 and the division disappears. For the unit vector u = (0.6, 0.8) and v = (5, 0), the dot product is v · u = 3, so the projection is 3u = (1.8, 2.4). This is one reason unit vectors are convenient: the number v · u is *exactly* how far v reaches along the line.

steps.headline: Projecting (3, 4) onto the line spanned by (2, 1)

lead.text: Find the coefficient, scale the direction, and then take the projection away from the vector to see what is left.

workedSteps.text: Dot v with d.
Dot d with itself.
Divide to get the coefficient.
Scale the direction by the coefficient to get the projection.
Subtract the projection from v to get the residual.
Check the right angle: the residual and d have dot product zero.

steps.headline: Projecting (4, 2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1)

lead.text: The two dot products are worked out, and the projection itself is yours.

workedSteps.text: Dot v with d, and d with itself.
Divide to get the coefficient, scale d by it, and read off the x coordinate of the projection.

steps.headline: Every vector splits into a part along a line and a part across it

lead.text: The projection and the residual add back to the original vector: v = proj + residual. The first part lies along the line and the second lies across it, at a right angle, so **the vector has been split into two perpendicular pieces**. For (3, 4) and the line spanned by (2, 1), the pieces are (4, 2) and (−1, 2), and indeed (4, 2) + (−1, 2) = (3, 4).

Because the pieces are perpendicular, Pythagoras's theorem applies to them: the square of the length of v is the sum of the squares of the lengths of the two pieces. Here the squared lengths are 25 for (3, 4), 20 for (4, 2) and 5 for (−1, 2), and 20 + 5 = 25. A vector that is *already* perpendicular to the line, such as (3, −3) for the line spanned by (1, 1), has no part along it at all, so its projection is the zero vector.

steps.headline: The projection really is the nearest point of the line

lead.text: Take any other point on the line, say c′d. The segment from v to c′d, the vector v − c′d, can be split as (v − p) + (p − c′d), where p is the projection. The first piece is the residual, which is perpendicular to the line, and the second lies along the line, so Pythagoras gives ‖v − c′d‖² = ‖v − p‖² + ‖p − c′d‖². The second term is positive unless c′d = p, so **every other point of the line is farther from v than p is**.

This is the property that makes projection useful beyond geometry. When a system of equations has no solution, because measurements disagree, the nearest vector that *can* be reached is a projection, and finding it is the idea behind fitting a line to noisy data in the next lesson.

lessons.orientation: Find the closest vector on a line and a perpendicular residual.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The line through the origin in the direction (2, 1) passes close to the point (1, 3) without touching it, and one point of the line is nearer to (1, 3) than any other. That point is found by dropping a perpendicular from (1, 3) to the line, so that the segment between them meets the line at a right angle, and in coordinates it comes from a single ratio of dot products.

The same question arises well beyond geometry. A system of equations with no solution, such as one built from noisy measurements, asks for a vector that cannot be reached, and the sensible response is to take the nearest vector that can be reached, which is found in the same way, by dropping a perpendicular. That is the idea behind fitting a line to data that do not lie on one.

intro.whyItMatters: Projection is the step that turns an unsolvable system into the best possible approximate answer.

recap.keyIdea: The projection of v onto the line spanned by d is ((v · d)/(d · d)) d, and the residual that remains is perpendicular to the line.

blocks.text: The projection is the nearest point of the line to v, found with two dot products and one scaling, and the residual is what is left. The two pieces are perpendicular, so their squared lengths add up to that of v, and a vector perpendicular to the line has projection zero.

recap.nextHook: Next, measurements that no line fits exactly are approximated by the nearest line, using the projection just met.

lessons.title: Fit with least squares

steps.headline: When no number matches every reading, the nearest one is a projection

lead.text: Take the readings 6, 7 and 11. A single value x that matched all three would need x = 6, x = 7 and x = 11 together, which is impossible, so the system has no solution. In vector form the readings are the vector b = (6, 7, 11), and the only vectors a single value can produce are the multiples x(1, 1, 1), which lie on one line. The best that can be done is to take the point of that line nearest to b, which is the projection of b onto (1, 1, 1), the idea of the last lesson in three dimensions.

Its coefficient is (b · (1, 1, 1)) ÷ ((1, 1, 1) · (1, 1, 1)) = (6 + 7 + 11) ÷ 3 = 8, which is the *mean* of the readings. Choosing the nearest point is called **least squares**, for a reason the next screen gives, and the explorer shows it for these readings and for a second set, 5, 6 and 10, whose mean is 7.

steps.headline: Least squares makes the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible

lead.text: Each reading misses the fit by a [[residual|What is left of a vector after its projection is taken away. Met in 'Project onto a direction'.]], the reading minus the fitted value. With the fit 8 the residuals of 6, 7 and 11 are −2, −1 and 3, and they are the entries of the residual vector b − 8(1, 1, 1). The squared length of that vector, 4 + 1 + 9 = 14, is the **sum of squared residuals**. The guess of 9 in the opening figure gives misses of −3, −2 and 2, and a sum of squares of 9 + 4 + 4 = 17, which is larger.

afterFigure.text: Squaring has three advantages. It removes the signs, so misses in opposite directions *cannot* cancel, it punishes a large miss more than several small ones, and it connects the problem to geometry: the projection is the point that makes the squared length of the residual smallest. **The residual is perpendicular to (1, 1, 1)**, so its entries add up to zero, as −2, −1 and 3 do, which is the property that makes the mean the balance point of the readings.

steps.headline: The residuals of the readings 2, 3 and 10

lead.text: Find the best constant, and then measure how far each reading is from it.

workedSteps.text: The best single value is the mean of the readings.
Subtract the fit from each reading to get the residuals.
The residuals add up to zero, as the residuals of a least-squares constant always do.
Square each residual and add them.

steps.headline: The sum of squared residuals for the fit 5

lead.text: Using the same measurements, 2, 4 and 9, and the same fit, 5, the residuals are set out and the squaring is yours.

workedSteps.text: The residuals are the measurements minus the fit.
Square each residual and add the three squares.

steps.headline: A line fitted to several points is again a projection

lead.text: A constant fits measurements badly when they rise or fall. A line y = c + sx has two unknowns, the intercept c and the slope s, and measurements at x = 0, 1 and 2 give three equations in them. Their coefficient matrix has columns (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 2), and the right-hand side is the vector of measurements b. When the three points are not on one line there is no exact solution, and the best fit is the projection of b onto the column space.

The residual b − Ax̂ must be perpendicular to both columns, which is the condition AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb, called the **normal equations**, where *normal* is an old word for perpendicular. For this matrix AᵀA has rows (3, 3) and (3, 5), and Aᵀb is the pair (Σy, Σxy). For heights 3, 3 and 6 these are 12 and 15, so 3c + 3s = 12 and 3c + 5s = 15, which give s = 1.5 and c = 2.5. The explorer shows this fit and a second one.

steps.headline: For three evenly spaced points the slope depends on the ends alone

lead.text: The two normal equations for measurements y₁, y₂ and y₃ at x = 0, 1 and 2 are 3c + 3s = y₁ + y₂ + y₃ and 3c + 5s = y₂ + 2y₃. Subtracting the first from the second leaves 2s = y₃ − y₁, so **s = (y₃ − y₁) ÷ 2**: the best slope is the rise from the first point to the last, divided by the two steps between them. With heights 3, 3 and 6 that gives (6 − 3) ÷ 2 = 1.5, as before, and the intercept follows from c = (mean of the y values) − s, because the fitted line passes through the mean point.

afterFigure.text: The shortcut holds *only* for three evenly spaced points, and the middle measurement affects the intercept but not the slope. A larger set of points needs the normal equations in full. When the points happen to lie exactly on a line, every residual is zero and the least-squares line is that line.

lessons.orientation: Fit inconsistent measurements by minimising squared residuals.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Three readings of the same quantity come out as 6, 7 and 11. A single value x that matched all three would have to satisfy x = 6, x = 7 and x = 11 together, and no number does, so the system has no solution. Some guesses for x still miss by less than others, since a guess of 9 is off by 3, 2 and 2 while a guess of 6 is off by 0, 1 and 5, and the problem is to choose the best one when an exact match is impossible.

The answer is to make the sum of the squares of the misses as small as possible. The choice has a geometric meaning, through the projections of the previous lesson, and it gives a method for fitting a straight line to any set of measurements. The method was published by Adrien-Marie Legendre in 1805, and Carl Friedrich Gauss, who said he had used it since 1795, gave his own account in 1809.

recap.keyIdea: Least squares fits inconsistent equations by projecting the measurements onto the column space, which minimises the sum of the squared residuals.

blocks.text: The least-squares constant is the mean of the readings, its residuals add to zero, and the best line satisfies the normal equations AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb. For three evenly spaced points the slope is the rise from the first to the last divided by two, and points that already lie on a line are fitted exactly.

recap.nextHook: Next, a set of independent directions is turned into perpendicular unit directions by subtracting projections.

lessons.title: Build an orthonormal basis

steps.headline: Against an orthonormal basis, coordinates are dot products

lead.text: Suppose u₁ and u₂ are [[orthonormal|Perpendicular vectors that each have length 1. Met in 'Orthogonal and unit vectors'.]], and write a vector as v = c₁u₁ + c₂u₂. Taking the dot product of both sides with u₁ gives v · u₁ = c₁(u₁ · u₁) + c₂(u₂ · u₁). The first dot product is 1, because u₁ has length 1, and the second is 0, because the two vectors are perpendicular, so c₁ = v · u₁, and in the *same* way c₂ = v · u₂. For u₁ = (0.6, 0.8), u₂ = (0.8, −0.6) and v = (5, 0), the dot products are 3 and 4, which are the amounts in the opening figure.

afterFigure.text: With a crooked pair such as (1, 1) and (1, 0), the dot product of which is 1 and not 0, the shortcut fails, since the two coordinates get tangled together, which is why solving a system was needed in the lesson on bases. The explorer shows the two kinds of pair. **An orthonormal basis turns finding coordinates into two multiplications**, and what remains is to build one.

steps.headline: Subtracting the projection leaves a vector perpendicular to the first

lead.text: Start with two independent vectors, a and b, which meet at some arbitrary angle. The part of b that lies along a can be removed with the projection of the previous lesson. For a = (1, 1) and b = (4, 7), the dot products are b · a = 11 and a · a = 2, so the projection is 5.5(1, 1), and what remains, b − 5.5a = (−1.5, 1.5), has dot product −1.5 + 1.5 = 0 with a. The explorer cuts the *same* b along the across axis, which leaves (0, 7), and along a.

afterFigure.text: The remainder is perpendicular to a because it is the residual of the projection, and it is not zero because b was not a multiple of a. **Subtracting the projection is the step that creates the right angle.** The remainder is still a combination of a and b, so the new direction lies in the same plane as the two original vectors.

steps.headline: Normalise, subtract, normalise: three moves build an orthonormal pair

lead.text: The construction is called the **Gram–Schmidt process**, after Jørgen Pedersen Gram, who used it in 1883, and Erhard Schmidt, who set it out in 1907. Given independent vectors a and b, first normalise a to get u₁. Second, subtract from b its part along u₁, which for a unit vector is just (b · u₁)u₁, leaving w = b − (b · u₁)u₁. Third, normalise w to get u₂.

Take a = (4, 3) and b = (3, 5). The length of a is 5, so u₁ = (0.8, 0.6). Then b · u₁ = 2.4 + 3 = 5.4, and w = (3, 5) − 5.4(0.8, 0.6) = (−1.32, 1.76), whose length is √(1.7424 + 3.0976) = √4.84 = 2.2. So u₂ = (−0.6, 0.8), and the explorer shows the part of b along (4, 3) and along the across axis.

afterFigure.text: The pair u₁ and u₂ is orthonormal, since (0.8, 0.6) · (−0.6, 0.8) = −0.48 + 0.48 = 0, and it spans the same plane as a and b. With a third vector the process continues in the same way: subtract the parts along *both* earlier unit vectors, and normalise what is left.

cases.label: The part of (3, 5) along the across axis

steps.headline: An orthonormal pair from (3, 4) and (7, 1)

lead.text: The two vectors are independent, so all three moves can be carried out.

workedSteps.text: Normalise the first vector. Its length is the square root of 3² + 4², which is 5.
Find how much of b lies along u₁ with a dot product.
Subtract that part from b.
The remainder is perpendicular to u₁, but its length is 5 and not 1, so normalise it.
Check the right angle.

steps.headline: Subtracting a projection when the direction is not a unit vector

lead.text: Take v = (1, 0) and u = (1, 1). The vector u has length √2, so the general formula divides by u · u. The coefficient is done, and the subtraction is yours.

workedSteps.text: Find the coefficient (v · u) ÷ (u · u).
Subtract 0.5u from v, and read the y coordinate of the remainder.

steps.headline: If the second vector adds nothing, the remainder is zero and cannot be normalised

lead.text: The process needs the second vector to bring something new. If b is a multiple of a, say a = (1, 2) and b = (3, 6), then the part of b along a is all of b, and the remainder is the zero vector, which has length zero and so *cannot* be normalised. The explorer shows this, and compares it with b = (3, 5), whose projection onto (1, 2) is (2.6, 5.2) and leaves the nonzero remainder (0.4, −0.2).

afterFigure.text: The process therefore doubles as **a test for independence**. A zero remainder at any stage means that the vector was a combination of the earlier ones, and so was dependent. The vectors of a basis are independent, so for a basis no stage can fail, and Gram–Schmidt turns any basis into an orthonormal one.

lessons.orientation: Subtract projections and normalise the remaining independent directions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Take the two vectors (0.6, 0.8) and (0.8, −0.6), which are at right angles and each of length 1. To write the vector (5, 0) as a combination of these two, you need only its dot product with each, and the two numbers that result, 3 and 4, are exactly the amounts required, since 3(0.6, 0.8) + 4(0.8, −0.6) = (5, 0), with no equations to solve.

Such a basis is rarely given in advance, but one can be built from any two independent vectors, by cutting from the second the part that lies along the first and scaling each piece to length 1, and with a basis built this way the coordinates of any vector are two dot products.

intro.whyItMatters: An orthonormal basis makes coordinates, projections and fits simple, and the next lessons rely on it.

recap.keyIdea: Gram–Schmidt builds an orthonormal basis by normalising the first vector, subtracting projections from each next one, and normalising what remains.

blocks.text: Subtracting the projection of b on a unit vector leaves a perpendicular remainder, and dividing that remainder by its length gives a unit vector at right angles to the first. A zero remainder shows that the vector was dependent, and against an orthonormal basis the coordinates of any vector are simply its dot products.

recap.nextHook: Next, some directions pass through a matrix unturned: they are only stretched, and they reveal what the matrix does.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

steps.headline: An eigenvector is a direction that a matrix only stretches

lead.text: A nonzero vector v is an **eigenvector** of a square matrix A if Av is a multiple of v, that is, if Av = λv for some number λ. The number λ is the **eigenvalue** belonging to v. For the matrix with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2), the vector (1, 0) goes to (3, 0) = 3(1, 0), so (1, 0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. The vector (1, −1) goes to (3 − 1, 0 − 2) = (2, −2) = 2(1, −1), so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2. The explorer shows both.

afterFigure.text: The prefix comes from the German word *eigen*, meaning own or characteristic: these are the directions that belong to the matrix. The vector must be **nonzero**, because A0 = 0 = λ0 holds for every λ and would say nothing. Any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector with the same eigenvalue, since A(cv) = cAv = λ(cv), so an eigenvector really names a whole line of directions.

steps.headline: A negative eigenvalue flips the direction, and a zero eigenvalue collapses it

lead.text: The eigenvalue says what happens along its line. A positive value stretches or shrinks the vectors on it, and a value of 1 leaves them where they are. The matrix with rows (0, 1) and (1, 0), which swaps the two coordinates, sends (1, 1) to (1, 1), with eigenvalue 1, and sends (1, −1) to (−1, 1) = −1(1, −1), with eigenvalue −1, so it reverses the vectors on that line. It is the reflection in the diagonal, and the two eigenvalues record it *exactly*.

A zero eigenvalue means that Av = 0 for a nonzero v, so v lies in the null space. The matrix with rows (1, 2) and (2, 4) sends (2, −1) to (0, 0), and sends (1, 2) to (5, 10) = 5(1, 2), so its eigenvalues are 0 and 5. **A square matrix has the eigenvalue 0 exactly when it is singular**, which links this lesson to the determinant and the null space.

steps.headline: Testing two directions for the matrix with rows (4, 1) and (2, 3)

lead.text: To test a candidate, apply the matrix and ask whether the output is a multiple of the input.

workedSteps.text: Apply the matrix to (1, 1), one row at a time.
The output is a multiple of the input, so (1, 1) is an eigenvector, and the multiplier is its eigenvalue.
Apply the matrix to (1, 0).
The input has no up part, but the output has one, so the output cannot be a multiple of it, and (1, 0) is not an eigenvector.

steps.headline: The eigenvalue for (1, −1)

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, −1). The output is worked out, and the eigenvalue is yours.

workedSteps.text: Apply the matrix to v, one row at a time.
Compare the output with v to find the multiplier λ.

steps.headline: A candidate passes if the output is a multiple of the input, in every coordinate

lead.text: Testing a candidate takes two steps: apply the matrix, and then check that **every coordinate of the output is the same multiple** of the matching coordinate of the input. For the matrix with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2), the candidate (0, 1) gives (1, 2), which cannot be a multiple of (0, 1) because its first coordinate is not zero, so (0, 1) is not an eigenvector. A coordinate of the input that is zero must give a zero in the output.

A matrix may also have no eigenvectors among real vectors at all. The quarter turn with rows (0, −1) and (1, 0) sends every vector to one at a right angle to it, so no vector stays on its *own* line. Eigenvectors exist when some direction is preserved, and finding them from scratch is the next question.

steps.headline: The eigenvalues are the values of λ that make det(A − λI) zero

lead.text: To find eigenvectors without guessing, rewrite Av = λv as (A − λI)v = 0. A nonzero solution v exists only if A − λI is singular, which happens **exactly when its determinant is zero**. For the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 2), this gives:

The eigenvalues are 1 and 3. For λ = 3 the matrix A − 3I has rows (−1, 1) and (1, −1), and its null space is spanned by (1, 1). For λ = 1 it has rows (1, 1) and (1, 1), with null space spanned by (1, −1). Each eigenvector is a null-space vector of A − λI, as the previous lessons made natural.

afterFigure.text: A check is available for a 2 × 2 matrix: the eigenvalues add up to the sum of the diagonal entries, 1 + 3 = 4, and multiply to the determinant, 1 × 3 = 3, which is 2 × 2 − 1 × 1. The equation for λ is a quadratic, so there are at most *two* eigenvalues for a 2 × 2 matrix.

lessons.orientation: Find nonzero directions that a square map changes only by a scalar.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The matrix with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2) sends the vector (1, 1) to (4, 2), which points in a different direction, so the matrix has turned the vector as well as stretching it. It sends (1, 0) to (3, 0), which lies on the same line through the origin and is simply three times as long.

Most vectors are turned by a matrix, so the directions that are only stretched are special, and they matter because along each of them the whole matrix reduces to multiplication by a single number. Knowing these directions and their stretch factors says what the matrix does in the simplest possible terms.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test whether a vector is an eigenvector, read its eigenvalue, and find the eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix.
intro.whyItMatters: Eigenvectors show what a matrix does along each direction, which is the key to powers of matrices and to decompositions.

recap.keyIdea: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a matrix only stretches, Av = λv, and its eigenvalues are the roots of det(A − λI) = 0.

blocks.text: To test a candidate, apply the matrix and check that the output is a multiple of the input, which gives the eigenvalue as the multiplier. A negative eigenvalue reverses the direction, a zero eigenvalue puts the vector in the null space, and for a 2 × 2 matrix the eigenvalues add to the trace, the sum of the diagonal entries, and multiply to the determinant.

recap.nextHook: Next, a basis of eigenvectors separates a matrix into independent stretches, which makes its powers easy to compute.

lessons.title: Diagonalise a map

steps.headline: Splitting a vector into eigenvector parts reduces the matrix to scalings

lead.text: The matrix A with rows (2, 1) and (1, 2) has the eigenvector (1, 1) with eigenvalue 3 and the eigenvector (1, −1) with eigenvalue 1. Applied to (0, 2) row by row, it mixes both coordinates and gives (2, 4). The same answer comes without mixing: split the vector along the eigenvectors, (0, 2) = 1(1, 1) − 1(1, −1), scale each part by its own eigenvalue, which gives 3 × 1(1, 1) − 1 × 1(1, −1) = (3, 3) − (1, −1) = (2, 4), and add the parts again. The explorer applies the matrix to (0, 2) and to (1, 1).

afterFigure.text: In general, if v = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ with v₁ and v₂ eigenvectors, then Av = c₁λ₁v₁ + c₂λ₂v₂, because the matrix respects sums and multiples and each eigenvector is *only* scaled. **In the eigenvector basis, the coordinates of v are simply scaled, each by its own eigenvalue.** When the eigenvectors form a basis the splitting is possible for every vector, since a basis gives every vector coordinates.

steps.headline: A = PDP⁻¹ says: find the coordinates, scale them, and convert back

lead.text: Collect the eigenvectors as the columns of a matrix P, and the eigenvalues, in the same order, along the diagonal of a matrix D that is zero elsewhere. For the matrix A above, P has columns (1, 1) and (1, −1), and D has the diagonal 3 and 1. Then:

lead.latex: A = P D P^{-1}, \qquad P = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}, \quad D = \begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \quad P^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}

lead.text: Read from the right, the formula gives three moves: P⁻¹ finds the coordinates of a vector in the eigenvector basis, D scales each coordinate by its eigenvalue, and P turns the scaled coordinates back into a vector. Multiplying P D P⁻¹ out gives the rows (2, 1) and (1, 2) again.

afterFigure.text: Writing A in this way is called **diagonalising** it, and A is *diagonalisable* when it can be done. The order matters: the first entry of D belongs to the first column of P, so swapping two columns of P means swapping the matching entries of D. P has to be invertible, so its columns must be independent, which means that they form a basis. The explorer shows the eigenvectors of the matrix with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2), which can be used in the same way.

steps.headline: Powers of a matrix only raise the eigenvalues to a power

lead.text: Applying A twice to an eigenvector multiplies it by its eigenvalue twice: A(Av) = A(λv) = λAv = λ²v. In general **Aᵏv = λᵏv**. For the vector (1, 1) of the matrix above, whose eigenvalue is 3, A²(1, 1) = 9(1, 1) and A¹⁰(1, 1) = 3¹⁰(1, 1) = 59049(1, 1).

The whole matrix behaves in the same way, since Aᵏ = P Dᵏ P⁻¹: in the product the inner P⁻¹P pairs cancel, and Dᵏ just raises each diagonal entry to the kth power. For k = 2, D² has the diagonal 9 and 1, and P D² P⁻¹ has the rows (5, 4) and (4, 5), which agrees with multiplying A by itself, since the first row of A² is (2 × 2 + 1 × 1, 2 × 1 + 1 × 2) = (5, 4).

afterFigure.text: Finding A¹⁰⁰ directly would take ninety-nine matrix multiplications, whereas the diagonal form needs only 3¹⁰⁰ and 1¹⁰⁰. This is how the long-run behaviour of a repeated process is read from eigenvalues: the eigenvalue with the largest size comes to *dominate*, because its power grows fastest.

steps.headline: Applying the matrix with rows (4, 1) and (2, 3) twice to (1, 1)

lead.text: The vector (1, 1) is an eigenvector of this matrix, so the second application need not be done row by row.

workedSteps.text: Apply A once. The output is a multiple of the input, so the eigenvalue is 5.
Apply A again. The matrix respects multiples, so the factor 5 can be taken outside.
Replace A(1, 1) by 5(1, 1) once more.
Two applications multiply the eigenvector by the eigenvalue squared.

steps.headline: Applying the matrix twice to (1, 1)

lead.text: Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and the vector (1, 1). The eigenvalue is found, and the second application is yours.

workedSteps.text: Apply A once.
Apply A a second time to find the scalar that multiplies (1, 1) in A²(1, 1).

steps.headline: A matrix without two independent eigenvectors cannot be diagonalised

lead.text: Diagonalising needs **a basis of eigenvectors**. The shear with rows (1, 1) and (0, 1) has the eigenvalue 1 only, since 1 is the root of (1 − λ)² = 0, and the eigenvectors are the null space of A − I, whose rows are (0, 1) and (0, 0). That null space contains *only* the multiples of (1, 0). The candidate (1, 1) goes to (2, 1), which is not a multiple of it, and the explorer shows both. Every eigenvector lies on one line, so there is no second independent column to put in P.

afterFigure.text: In such a case P cannot be invertible and the matrix is not diagonalisable. Two different eigenvalues always give two independent eigenvectors, so the trouble arises only when eigenvalues repeat, as with the shear, or when they are not real, as with a quarter turn. A matrix that fails has a more complicated standard form, which this course does not go into.

lessons.orientation: Use an eigenvector basis to separate a square map into independent scalings.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 2) mixes the coordinates of every vector it touches: applied to (0, 2) it gives (2, 4), and each output coordinate depends on both input coordinates. The same result can be reached without any mixing, because (0, 2) is the sum of (1, 1) and (−1, 1), which lie along the two special directions of this matrix, and the matrix triples the first part and leaves the second unchanged, so that (3, 3) + (−1, 1) gives (2, 4) again.

That observation is the idea behind diagonalising a map, which reduces a matrix to a list of separate stretches and makes some otherwise laborious questions easy, such as what happens when the matrix is applied a hundred times.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write a matrix as PDP⁻¹, read the diagonal of D, find powers of a matrix, and say when this is impossible.
intro.whyItMatters: Diagonalisation reduces a matrix to separate scalings, which is how repeated processes and many physical systems are analysed.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix with a basis of eigenvectors can be written as PDP⁻¹, which scales each coordinate in that basis and makes powers easy.

blocks.text: The columns of P are independent eigenvectors and D carries their eigenvalues in matching order, so Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ and an eigenvector is multiplied by λᵏ. If the eigenvectors lie on a single line, as with the shear, P cannot be invertible and the matrix cannot be diagonalised.

recap.nextHook: Next, the same idea of separating a map into independent stretches is extended to matrices that are not square, which leads to the singular value decomposition.

lessons.title: Singular value decomposition

steps.headline: Some matrices are a stretch followed by a turn

lead.text: Return to the matrix A with rows (0, −3) and (5, 0). Its columns, (0, 5) and (−3, 0), are perpendicular and have lengths 5 and 3, so A stretches the across direction by 5 and the up direction by 3 and then turns the whole plane a quarter turn, which sends (5, 0) to (0, 5) and (0, 3) to (−3, 0). The stretch sizes, 5 and 3, are called the **singular values** of A. The explorer shows this matrix, and the plain stretch with rows (5, 0) and (0, 3), which has the *same* singular values and no turn.

afterFigure.text: A turn changes no length and no angle, so the lengths of the outputs depend on the stretch alone. The longest output that A gives for an input of length 1 has length 5, the largest singular value, and the shortest has length 3. **A turn moves vectors around, and only the stretch changes their size.**

steps.headline: Every matrix is a turn, a stretch and a second turn: A = UΣVᵀ

lead.text: In general a matrix is not one stretch followed by one turn, but a turn, then a stretch, then a second turn. The first turn is Vᵀ, which lines the input up with a set of perpendicular directions, Σ then stretches along them, and U turns the result. In symbols:

The matrices U and V are **orthogonal**: their columns are orthonormal, so each turns or reflects space without changing a length or an angle. The matrix Σ is diagonal, with the singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … on its diagonal, all at least zero. This is the *singular value decomposition*, or SVD, which Eugenio Beltrami found for real square matrices in 1873 and Camille Jordan found independently in 1874.

afterFigure.text: A negative stretch never needs to appear, because a flip can always be placed inside U or V. The matrix with rows (−5, 0) and (0, 1) has singular values 5 and 1, with the flip in U, as the explorer shows beside the plain stretch. The singular values are also the square roots of the [[eigenvalues|Numbers λ with Av = λv for some nonzero v. Met in 'Eigenvectors and eigenvalues'.]] of AᵀA, which is how they are computed: for the matrix with rows (0, −3) and (5, 0), AᵀA has rows (25, 0) and (0, 9), with eigenvalues 25 and 9.

steps.headline: The SVD of the matrix with rows (−4, 0) and (0, 2)

lead.text: A diagonal matrix with a negative entry is the simplest case in which a sign has to be accounted for.

workedSteps.text: The columns are perpendicular, with lengths 4 and 2, so these are the singular values.
Σ holds the singular values in decreasing order.
A negative stretch is not allowed in Σ, so the flip goes into U, which reverses the across direction.
With V the identity, the product UΣ returns the original matrix.

steps.headline: The number of nonzero singular values is the rank

lead.text: A direction that a matrix flattens has a singular value of zero, so **the number of nonzero singular values is the [[rank|The number of pivots of a matrix: the dimension of its column space. Met in 'Rank and null space'.]] of the matrix**. The matrix with *every* entry equal to 1 sends every vector to a multiple of (1, 1), so its rank is 1, and its singular values are 2 and 0. The identity matrix changes nothing, so both of its singular values are 1. The explorer shows both matrices.

afterFigure.text: For a square matrix a zero singular value goes with a determinant of zero: the plane has been collapsed onto a line, and there is no inverse. The size of the smallest singular value therefore measures how close a matrix is to being singular, which is why numerical software keeps an eye on it.

steps.headline: The singular values of the matrix with rows (1, 2) and (2, 4)

lead.text: The rank decides how many singular values are nonzero, and the smaller one is yours to find.

workedSteps.text: The second column, (2, 4), is twice the first, (1, 2), so the columns lie on one line and the rank is 1.
Use the rank to decide how many singular values can be nonzero, and state the smaller one.

steps.headline: The decomposition works for matrices that are not square

lead.text: Nothing in the construction needs the matrix to be square. If A has m rows and n columns, then Vᵀ is n × n and turns the inputs, Σ is m × n and stretches while *changing the number of coordinates*, and U is m × m and turns the outputs. Σ carries the singular values on its main diagonal, as many as the smaller of m and n, and zeros elsewhere. The matrix with rows (3, 0), (0, 1) and (0, 0) takes the plane into three-dimensional space by stretching by 3 and 1, and the explorer shows it beside a square example.

afterFigure.text: Because the singular values are listed from largest to smallest, keeping only the largest few gives **the best approximation of the matrix by one of lower rank**, a result of Carl Eckart and Gale Young from 1936. That is why the SVD is used to compress images and to find the strongest patterns in large tables of data.

lessons.orientation: Separate a rectangular map into orthogonal coordinate changes and nonnegative stretches.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The matrix with rows (0, −3) and (5, 0) sends (1, 0) to (0, 5) and (0, 1) to (−3, 0), so the unit square becomes a rectangle with sides 5 and 3. This matrix has no eigenvectors among real vectors, since it turns every direction, so the diagonal form of the last lesson is out of reach. Yet its action could hardly be simpler: a stretch by 5 in one direction and by 3 in the perpendicular direction, followed by a turn.

Every matrix, square or not, can be described in that way, as a turn, a stretch along perpendicular directions, and a second turn. The sizes of the stretches say at a glance how much the matrix enlarges space and how many directions it flattens.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the singular values of a matrix, say what each factor of A = UΣVᵀ does, and give the shape of Σ for a rectangular matrix.
intro.whyItMatters: The decomposition shows what any matrix does to space, and it underlies data compression and the search for the strongest patterns in data.

recap.keyIdea: Every matrix factors as UΣVᵀ: a turn, a stretch by the nonnegative singular values, and a second turn, whatever the matrix's shape.

blocks.text: U and V are orthogonal, so they move vectors without changing lengths, and Σ is diagonal with the singular values in decreasing order. The largest singular value is the greatest stretch, the number of nonzero singular values is the rank, and a rectangular matrix has a Σ of the same shape as itself.

questions.prompt: For v = (3, −2), what is the x coordinate?
hints: Which of the two numbers comes first?
x is the across coordinate, and the pair is written (x, y).
Read the first number, keeping its sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate is 3; the second is −2.

questions.onCorrect: x is the first number. The −2 belongs to y and sends the vector downwards.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second coordinate, y. The x coordinate comes first.

questions.prompt: Are (3, 7) and (7, 3) the same vector?
hints: Compare the first numbers, then the second numbers.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The x coordinates differ, so the vectors differ.

questions.onCorrect: The first coordinates are 3 and 7, so the vectors differ even though they use the same two numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: They use the same two numbers, but in different places. The position of each number matters.

questions.prompt: How many units across does the move (0, −6) take you?
hints: Which coordinate says how far across?
A coordinate of zero means no movement in that direction.
The −6 is the up-and-down part, not the across part.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate is 0, so the move goes 0 units across; the −6 sends it 6 units down.

questions.onCorrect: The first coordinate is 0, so the move is straight down, 6 units, with no movement across.

misconceptions.feedback: −6 is the second coordinate, which says how far up or down. The first coordinate says how far across.
6 is the size of the second coordinate, which is the movement down. The first coordinate says how far across.

questions.prompt: How many units up does the move (0, 1) take you?
hints: Which position in the pair says how far up?
The pair is (across, up).
Read the second number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate is the up distance, and it is 1.

questions.onCorrect: The second number is the distance up, so (0, 1) goes straight up by 1 and not at all across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the across number. The up number is the second one.

questions.prompt: Give the x coordinate of (−5, 3).
hints: Which position names x?
Coordinates are ordered (x, y). Keep the sign you read.
Report the first entry, including its minus sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate is −5.

questions.onCorrect: −5. The sign is part of the coordinate: it means 5 units the other way across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is y, the second coordinate. x is the first number, with its sign.
Check the sign. A minus sign is part of the coordinate.

questions.prompt: Give the y coordinate of (6, −4).
hints: Which position names y?
Coordinates are ordered (x, y).
Report the second entry, keeping its sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate is −4.

questions.onCorrect: −4. y is the second number, and its minus sign says the vector goes down.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x, the first coordinate. y is the second number.
The sign is missing. Read the minus sign along with the number.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of (2, 1) + (−1, 3)?
hints: Which coordinate does the question ask for?
Combine only the across entries, with their signs.
Add the first entry of each vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The x coordinate is 2 + (−1) = 1.

questions.onCorrect: Add the across entries, signs included: 2 + (−1). The up entries do not mix in.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the second entry from the first. The sum adds the two across entries as written.
That multiplies the two across entries. Add them.

questions.prompt: What is the y coordinate of 3(2, −1)?
hints: Which entry is the y coordinate?
Multiply it by the scalar, keeping its sign.
A positive scalar times a negative number gives a negative number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The y coordinate is 3 × (−1) = −3.

questions.onCorrect: Multiply every coordinate by the scalar: 3 × (−1) = −3.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales the x coordinate. The question asks for y.
That is y before scaling. Multiply it by the scalar.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of −2(2, −1)?
hints: Apply the scalar to the first coordinate.
A negative scalar flips the sign of what it multiplies.
Multiply the first entry by the negative scalar.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate becomes −2 × 2 = −4.

questions.onCorrect: A negative scalar flips the sign and stretches: −2 × 2 = −4.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. A negative scalar times a positive entry is negative.
That adds the scalar to the entry. A scalar multiplies.

questions.prompt: The move (3, 2) is followed by the move (−3, −2). How far up from its start does the path end?
hints: Add the up parts of the two moves.
One move went up and the other came back down.
Add the second entries, with their signs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The vertical movements add to 2 − 2 = 0.

questions.onCorrect: The up parts are 2 and −2, which add to 0. Moves in opposite directions cancel, so the path ends level with where it began.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes and ignores the sign. The second move goes the other way.

questions.prompt: Let u = (2, 1) and v = (−1, 3). What is the y coordinate of 2u + v?
hints: Scale u before adding v.
Double each entry of u, then add the matching entries of v.
Double the second entry of u, then add the second entry of v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First 2u = (4, 2); adding v gives (3, 5), so y = 5.

questions.onCorrect: Double u to get (4, 2). Adding v entry by entry gives (3, 5), so y is 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is u + v, where u was not doubled first.
That doubles v as well. Only u gets the scalar.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of (4, 1) − (1, 3)?
hints: Subtracting works entry by entry, like adding.
Take the second vector's across entry away from the first's.
Subtract the first entries.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtract matching entries: the first is 4 − 1 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Subtract entry by entry, first vector first: 4 − 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the entries. The question subtracts.
That subtracts in the wrong order. The first vector comes first.

hints: Multiply matching coordinates, then add.
The first product is positive and the second is negative.
Add the two products, keeping the sign of each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dot product is 2 × 3 + 1 × (−2) = 6 − 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 6 + (−2) = 4. The result is one number: both signed products added.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign of the second product: one of its two entries is negative.

questions.prompt: A vector goes 3 across and 4 up. What is its length?
hints: Picture the right-angled triangle the vector makes.
Square each coordinate, add the squares, then take the square root.
Which whole number multiplied by itself gives the sum of the squares?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The squared length is 9 + 16 = 25, so the length is 5.

questions.onCorrect: Square, add, then take the square root: √(9 + 16) = 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the coordinates. Square them first.
That is the sum of the squares. The length is its square root.

hints: Multiply matching entries, then add.
A negative times a negative is positive.
The two products are both positive. Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products are 1 and 4, which sum to 5.

questions.onCorrect: The products are 1 and 4. A vector dotted with itself is never negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The second product is (−2) × (−2), which is positive. Check its sign.

questions.prompt: A displacement is (−6, 8) kilometres. How many kilometres is the end from the start?
hints: Distance is the length of the vector.
Square each coordinate and add. The minus sign disappears.
Take the positive square root of the sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sum of squares is 36 + 64 = 100, whose square root is 10.

questions.onCorrect: The squares 36 and 64 sum to 100, and the square root is 10. The signs of the coordinates do not change the length.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the squares. The distance is its square root.
That adds the coordinates. Square them first.

hints: Multiply matching coordinates.
The second product has a negative entry in it.
Add the two signed products.
questions.onCorrect: 2 + (−12) = −10. A dot product can be negative when the vectors disagree.

misconceptions.feedback: The second product is (−3) × 4, which is negative. Keep its sign.

questions.prompt: Find the length of (5, 12).
hints: Square both coordinates.
Add the two squares.
Take the positive square root of the sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sum of squares is 25 + 144 = 169, giving length 13.

questions.onCorrect: √(25 + 144) = 13. Length is the root of the vector's dot product with itself.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the squares. The length is its square root.
That adds the coordinates. Square them first.

hints: Multiply matching coordinates.
One product is negative.
Add the two products. Do they cancel?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products −2 and 2 cancel, so the vectors are orthogonal.

questions.onCorrect: The products cancel, so the dot product is zero. Zero means orthogonal.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign of the first product: one of its entries is negative.

questions.prompt: A unit vector in the direction (3, 4) has what x coordinate?
hints: Find the vector's length first.
Divide the x coordinate by the length.
Write the fraction as a decimal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The length is 5, so the first unit coordinate is 3/5 = 0.6.

questions.onCorrect: 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. Divide each coordinate by the length.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the coordinate before dividing by the length.
That is the y coordinate. The question asks for x.

questions.prompt: The vectors (2, 0) and (0, 3) are:
hints: Check the dot product, then check both lengths.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their dot product is zero, but their lengths are 2 and 3, not 1.

questions.onCorrect: The dot product is zero, so they are orthogonal. Their lengths are not 1, so not orthonormal.

misconceptions.feedback: Orthonormal needs unit length as well. Check how long each vector is.
Their dot product is zero, so they are orthogonal.

questions.prompt: Can a direction be found for the zero vector (0, 0) by dividing it by its length?
hints: Work out its length before trying to divide.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Its length is zero, and you cannot divide by zero.

questions.onCorrect: No. The length of (0, 0) is zero, and dividing by zero is not possible. The zero vector has no direction to record.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the length of (0, 0). You cannot divide by that.

hints: Multiply corresponding coordinates.
The second product is negative.
Add the two products. Do they cancel?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products 2 and −2 add to zero.

questions.onCorrect: 2 + (−2) = 0, so these vectors are orthogonal.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign of the second product: one entry is negative.

questions.prompt: A unit vector in the direction (0, −7) has what y coordinate?
hints: Find the length first. It is positive.
Divide the y coordinate by the length.
A negative number divided by a positive number is negative.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Its length is 7; the second unit coordinate is −7/7 = −1.

questions.onCorrect: −7 ÷ 7 = −1. This vector already points along an axis, so its unit vector is that axis direction.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the coordinate before dividing by the length.
The sign is missing. A negative coordinate divided by a positive length stays negative.

questions.prompt: The matrix A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ has one row for each sensor and one column for each hour of readings. How many sensors does it describe?
hints: Each row is a sensor.
Count the rows.
Rows run across the matrix.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are two rows, and each row is a sensor.

questions.onCorrect: Each row is one sensor and A has two rows, so it describes two sensors. The three columns are the hours.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of hours, which are the columns.

questions.prompt: A has 2 rows and 3 columns. How many entries must v have for A v to make sense?
hints: Each row of A pairs up with v, entry by entry.
How many entries does one row of A have?
A row is as long as the matrix has columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A has three columns, so each row has three entries and v needs three entries.

questions.onCorrect: Each row of A pairs with v entry by entry, so v needs one entry per column.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows. Each row has as many entries as there are columns.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ comes from entry (2, 3) of A.
Look in the second row and the third column of A.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A, which is 5.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the positions: entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A.

misconceptions.feedback: That is entry (2, 2) of A. Swap the two positions as written.
That is entry (1, 2) of A. Swap the positions, then read the row and column.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, how many columns does Aᵀ have?
hints: Rows of A become columns of Aᵀ.
Count the rows of A.
The number of rows of A is the number of columns of Aᵀ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A has two rows, so Aᵀ has two columns.

questions.onCorrect: A has two rows, and each becomes a column of Aᵀ.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of columns of A. The transpose swaps rows and columns.

questions.prompt: Let B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\7&3\\4&0\end{pmatrix}$. What is entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ comes from entry (1, 2) of B.
Look in the first row and the second column of B.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: This is the original entry (1, 2), which is −1.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the positions: entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ is entry (1, 2) of B.

misconceptions.feedback: That is entry (2, 1) of B itself. Swap the positions first.

questions.prompt: A has 3 rows and 2 columns. How many columns does Aᵀ have?
hints: Rows and columns swap.
Which count of A becomes the columns of Aᵀ?
The rows of A become the columns of Aᵀ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The transpose's column count is the original row count: 3.

questions.onCorrect: The transpose swaps the counts, so its columns number as many as A's rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of columns of A. The transpose swaps rows and columns.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 2), what is the first coordinate of A v?
hints: Which row gives the first output entry?
Multiply each row entry by the matching entry of v, then add.
Dot the first row with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first row gives 2 × 1 + 1 × 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The first row dotted with v gives the first output entry: 2 × 1 + 1 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the first column of A. Use the first row for the first output entry.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is the second coordinate of A(1, 0)?
hints: Use the second row of A.
Multiply each entry of that row by the matching input entry, then add.
The input has a zero in it, so one term disappears.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first column is (1, 3), so the second coordinate is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The input (1, 0) selects the first column of A, so the output is that column.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of the output. The question asks for the second.

questions.prompt: For a linear T, which expression always equals T(u + v)?
hints: Apply the map to both vectors, then combine.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A linear map keeps sums: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v).

questions.onCorrect: A linear map keeps sums: mapping the sum is the same as summing the maps.

misconceptions.feedback: A dot product gives a number, not a vector. Linear maps keep sums.
Both vectors should be mapped. Only T(u) + T(v) treats them alike.

questions.prompt: Is the shift S(v) = v + (1, 0), which moves every vector 1 unit across, a linear transformation?
hints: Find S(0, 0) and see where zero goes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. S sends zero to (1, 0), but a linear map keeps zero at zero.

questions.onCorrect: No. S sends the zero vector to (1, 0), and a linear map always keeps zero at zero.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the zero vector. A linear map must send it to zero, and this one moves it.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is the first coordinate of A(2, 1)?
hints: Use the first row of A.
Multiply each row entry by the matching input entry, then add.
Dot the first row with the input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first row gives 1 × 2 + 2 × 1 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Row dotted with input: 1 × 2 + 2 × 1 gives the first output entry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second coordinate of the output. The question asks for the first.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, what is the second coordinate of A(−1, 4)?
hints: Use the second row of A.
Keep the negative entry in the row.
Dot the second row with the input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second row gives 0 × (−1) − 2 × 4 = −8.

questions.onCorrect: Second row dotted with the input: 0 × (−1) + (−2) × 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of the output. The question asks for the second.
The sign is missing. The row entry is negative and the input entry is positive.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A B? Count from 1.
hints: Pair the first row of A with the second column of B.
Multiply matching positions, then add.
The row is (1, 2). Dot it with the column.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dot product is 1 × 0 + 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: Row 1 of A dotted with column 2 of B: 1 × 0 + 2 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses column 1 of B. The question names column 2.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of B A? Count from 1.
hints: B is now the left matrix, so it gives the row.
Pair the first row of B with the second column of A.
Multiply matching positions, then add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first row (2, 0) and second column (2, 1) give 4.

questions.onCorrect: Row 1 of B dotted with column 2 of A: 2 × 2 + 0 × 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the same entry of A B. In B A, matrix B goes first.
