questions.prompt: A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2. What is the shape of A B?
hints: Keep the outer numbers and drop the matching inner ones.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2 × 3 times 3 × 2 gives 2 × 2: the inner 3s match and vanish.

questions.onCorrect: The inner 3s match and vanish. A B has A's rows and B's columns: 2 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That would use the inner numbers. They match and disappear; the outer numbers stay.
That is the shape of A. The product has A's rows and B's columns.

questions.prompt: Which map acts first in A B v?
hints: Read the expression from the inside out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: B acts first, since A B v means A(B v).

questions.onCorrect: A B v means A(B v). The matrix next to v acts first.

misconceptions.feedback: A acts on the result of B v, so it comes second. The matrix nearest v acts first.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 1) of A B? Count from 1.
hints: Use the second row of A and the first column of B.
Multiply matching positions, then add.
One of the products involves a zero.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Row (1, 0) dotted with column (1, 2) gives 1 × 1 + 0 × 2 = 1.

questions.onCorrect: Row 2 of A dotted with column 1 of B: 1 × 1 + 0 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the second column of B. The question asks for the first.

questions.prompt: Which identity holds for any matrices A and B that can be multiplied?
hints: Transposing a product reverses the order of its factors.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (A B)ᵀ = Bᵀ Aᵀ: the order reverses.

questions.onCorrect: A transpose reverses a product: the last factor's transpose comes first.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps the order. Transposing reverses it, like taking off shoes and socks.

questions.prompt: The 2 × 2 identity matrix sends every vector to itself. What is its inverse?
hints: What does the identity matrix do to a vector?
Undoing a map that does nothing requires no change.
Which matrix X satisfies X I = I?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The identity matrix itself, because undoing a map that changes nothing means changing nothing again.

choices.label: It has no inverse, because there is nothing to undo
The identity matrix with every sign changed

questions.onCorrect: The identity does nothing, so undoing it means doing nothing again: I times I is I, which makes the identity its own inverse.

misconceptions.feedback: Changing every sign gives −I, which sends each vector v to −v. Its product with I is −I and not I, so it reverses vectors instead of leaving them where they were.
The zero matrix sends every vector to the zero vector, so it cannot give the original vector back. A matrix that undoes I has to leave every vector as it is.
A map that changes nothing can still be undone, by changing nothing again, since I times I is I. Only maps that send different vectors to the same output cannot be undone.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: Find ad − bc first.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the others, then divide by that number.
Which diagonal entry of A lands in the position the question names?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inverse is [(1, −1); (−1, 2)]. Multiplying it by A gives I.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the diagonal entries and divide by ad − bc, which is 1 here.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a different diagonal entry. The two diagonal entries swap places.

questions.prompt: Does A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ have an inverse?
hints: Find ad − bc.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. ad − bc = 4 − 4 = 0.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc = 1 × 4 − 2 × 2 = 0, so there is no inverse.

misconceptions.feedback: Work out ad − bc. A zero there means no inverse.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, the vector v satisfies A v = (1, −2). What is the first coordinate of v?
hints: Write out what A v equals, one row at a time.
The second row gives the second coordinate of v on its own.
Put that value into the first row and solve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second equation gives v₂ = −1. The first gives v₁ − 1 = 1, hence v₁ = 2.

questions.onCorrect: The second row gives 2 × v₂ = −2, so v₂ = −1. The first row then gives v₁ − 1 = 1, so v₁ = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of the output, not of the input.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: What does A do to a point? It slides it sideways.
To undo a sideways slide, slide back by the same amount.
The inverse slides the opposite way. Negate the entry in the top right of A.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inverse subtracts the shear: [(1, −2); (0, 1)].

questions.onCorrect: Negate the off-diagonal entry: the inverse shear goes the other way.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The off-diagonal entries are negated.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: The matrix scales each axis separately.
Undo a multiplication by dividing by the same number.
Take the reciprocal of the matching diagonal entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Undo multiplication by −2 with multiplication by −1/2.

questions.onCorrect: Undo multiplying by −2 by multiplying by −1/2. Diagonal matrices invert entry by entry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the entry of A itself. The inverse entry is its reciprocal.
The sign is missing. Undoing a negative scale is still negative.

questions.prompt: For x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ − x₂ = 1, what is x₁?
hints: Add the two equations together.
Which unknown disappears when you add?
Divide by the coefficient that is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adding the equations gives 3x₁ = 6, so x₁ = 2.

questions.onCorrect: Adding the equations cancels x₂ and leaves one unknown to solve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x₂. Check which unknown the question asks for.
That is the value of 3x₁, before dividing by its coefficient.

questions.prompt: Starting from x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ − x₂ = 1, perform R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁. What is the new right side of row 2?
hints: Take twice the first row's right-hand side away from the second row's.
Multiply the first right-hand side by the multiplier.
Subtract that from the second right-hand side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new right side is 1 − 2 × 5 = −9.

questions.onCorrect: Apply the operation to every entry, right side included: 1 − 2 × 5 = −9.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes row 1's right side away once. The operation subtracts it twice.
That adds twice the first row. The operation subtracts.

questions.prompt: In the reduced system x₁ + x₂ = 5 and −3x₂ = −9, what is x₂?
hints: Which equation has only one unknown?
Divide both sides by the coefficient of x₂.
A negative divided by a negative is positive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dividing −3x₂ = −9 by −3 gives x₂ = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Solve the one-unknown row first: divide both sides by the coefficient of x₂.

misconceptions.feedback: The signs cancel when you divide a negative by a negative.

questions.prompt: The first equation is x₂ = 5 and the second is x₁ + x₂ = 4. What is x₁?
hints: One equation already tells you x₂.
Put that value into the other equation.
Subtract it from the right-hand side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first equation gives x₂ = 5. Then x₁ + 5 = 4, so x₁ = −1.

questions.onCorrect: Start with the simplest equation, then substitute into the other.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x₂. Put it into the other equation to find x₁.

questions.prompt: Solve x₁ + x₂ = 5, x₂ + x₃ = 4 and x₃ = 1. What is x₁?
hints: Which equation has only one unknown?
Work up from the bottom, one unknown at a time.
Find x₂ from the middle equation, then x₁ from the top.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Read x₃ = 1, then x₂ = 3, then x₁ = 2.

questions.onCorrect: Work up from the bottom: each solved unknown goes into the equation above it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x₃. Keep working up to x₁.
That is x₂. Put it into the first equation for x₁.

questions.prompt: Solve 2x₁ + x₂ = 8 and x₁ − x₂ = 1. What is x₂?
hints: Add the two equations together.
The x₂ terms cancel. Solve for x₁ first.
Put the value of x₁ into the second equation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equations give x₁ = 3 and x₂ = 2; both original equations check.

questions.onCorrect: Adding cancels x₂, giving x₁. Substituting back gives x₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x₁. Put it into an equation to find x₂.

questions.prompt: How many solutions do x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3 have?
hints: Does either equation contradict the other, or leave an unknown free?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each unknown is fixed by its own equation: exactly one solution.

questions.onCorrect: Each equation fixes one unknown, with no conflict and nothing free: exactly one solution.

misconceptions.feedback: Both equations can be true at once: each one fixes a different unknown.
Each unknown is pinned down by its own equation, so nothing is left free.

questions.prompt: How many solutions do x₁ + x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 7 have?
hints: Subtract twice the first equation from the second. What does the remaining row say?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reduced second row reads 0 = 1, which is impossible.

questions.onCorrect: Reduce it and the second row reads 0 = 1: a contradiction.

misconceptions.feedback: Two equations that are multiples of each other on the left cannot pin down two unknowns.
Check the right sides. The second would need to be double the first for the equations to agree.

questions.prompt: How many solutions do x₁ + x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 6 have?
hints: Subtract twice the first equation from the second. What is left?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second equation is double the first, so one unknown is free: infinitely many solutions.

questions.onCorrect: The second equation adds nothing, so one unknown stays free: infinitely many solutions.

misconceptions.feedback: The second equation is just double the first, so it adds no new restriction.
Check the right sides. They agree here: the second equation is exactly double the first.

questions.prompt: A consistent system has x₁ + x₃ = 3 and x₂ + 2x₃ = 4. How many free variables does it have?
hints: Count the unknowns, then count the pivot columns.
Free variables are the columns left without a pivot.
Subtract the number of pivots from the number of unknowns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three variable columns and two pivots, leaving one free variable.

questions.onCorrect: Unknowns minus pivots: three variable columns less two pivots leaves one free variable.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pivots. Free variables are the columns left over.
That counts all the unknowns. Only columns without a pivot are free.

questions.prompt: Does every system A x = 0 include the zero vector as a solution?
hints: Put x = 0 into A x and see what comes out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A times the zero vector is always the zero vector.

questions.onCorrect: A times the zero vector is always zero, so x = 0 solves every system A x = 0.

misconceptions.feedback: Try x = 0. Every entry of A x is a sum of products with zero, so the result is zero.

questions.prompt: How many free variables remain in x₁ + 2x₂ + 3x₃ = 0?
hints: How many unknowns, and how many equations?
One equation can fix only one unknown.
Subtract the number of pivots from the number of unknowns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One independent equation restricts three variables, leaving two free variables.

questions.onCorrect: Three unknowns, one pivot: two free variables, each able to take any value.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the equations. Free variables are the unknowns left over.
That counts all the unknowns. One of them is fixed by the equation.

questions.prompt: The vectors (1, 2) and (2, 4) are combined in every possible way, by scaling each and adding the results. What shape do the results form?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare the second vector with double the first.
If one is a scaled copy, it adds no new direction.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A line through the origin, because (2, 4) is twice (1, 2) and adds no new direction.

questions.onCorrect: Since (2, 4) = 2(1, 2), every combination is a multiple of (1, 2), so the span is a line through the origin and has dimension 1.

misconceptions.feedback: Since (2, 4) = 2(1, 2), every combination c₁(1, 2) + c₂(2, 4) equals (c₁ + 2c₂)(1, 2), a multiple of (1, 2), so the results stay on one line.
The combinations include (1, 2) itself and all of its multiples, so there are many points. The origin is only the combination in which both coefficients are zero.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (1, 0) and (1, 1)?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare their directions.
Two vectors in different directions span a plane.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: They are not scalar multiples, so they span a two-dimensional plane.

questions.onCorrect: Two vectors in different directions span the whole plane.

misconceptions.feedback: The second vector is not a multiple of the first, so it adds a new direction.

questions.prompt: Is the set of points (x, y) with y = 2x a subspace of the plane?
hints: Is it a span of one vector? Does it contain zero?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. It is the span of (1, 2), so it contains zero and is closed.

questions.onCorrect: It is all multiples of (1, 2): a span, so a subspace.

misconceptions.feedback: That set is the span of (1, 2). Every span is a subspace.

questions.prompt: Is the set of points (x, y) with y = 2x + 1 a subspace of the plane?
hints: Does the set contain the zero vector?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The point (0, 0) gives y = 0, not 1, so zero is not in the set.

questions.onCorrect: Zero is not on the path, and every subspace must contain it.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the zero vector. A subspace must contain it.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (2, 1) and (−4, −2)?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare the second vector with the first.
A negative multiple still lies on the same line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second vector is −2 times the first, so they span one line.

questions.onCorrect: A negative multiple points back along the same line, so the span is one line.

misconceptions.feedback: Check whether the second vector is a multiple of the first. It is.

questions.prompt: Write (5, 3) = c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1). What is c₁?
hints: Match the second coordinates first.
Then match the first coordinates.
The first coordinate of the combination is c₁ plus c₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate gives c₂ = 3; the first then gives c₁ = 2.

questions.onCorrect: Match coordinates one at a time: c₂ from the second, then c₁ from the first.

misconceptions.feedback: That is c₂. Put it into the first coordinates to find c₁.
That adds c₂ to the target. The target is c₁ plus c₂, so subtract.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest number of vectors that can span the whole plane?
hints: How many directions does one vector's span reach?
One vector spans only a line.
Two vectors that are not multiples of each other reach every point.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One vector spans only a line, and two independent vectors span the whole plane, so the smallest number is two.

questions.onCorrect: One vector reaches only a line, so the plane needs two, and the next screen gives such a smallest spanning set its name.

misconceptions.feedback: Three vectors can span the plane, but one of them would be redundant: it would be a combination of the other two.

questions.prompt: Do (1, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1) form a basis for the plane?
hints: Is any of the three a combination of the other two?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. (1, 1) is the sum of the other two, so the set has a redundant vector.

questions.onCorrect: The third vector is the sum of the first two, so the set is redundant: not a basis.

misconceptions.feedback: The third vector is the sum of the first two. A basis cannot contain that redundancy.

questions.prompt: Write (6, 4) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1). What is c₁?
hints: Match the first coordinates, then the second.
You get two equations in c₁ and c₂.
Add the two equations so that c₂ cancels.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equations are c₁ + c₂ = 6 and c₁ − c₂ = 4. Adding gives 2c₁ = 10, so c₁ = 5.

questions.onCorrect: Match coordinates to get two equations, then add them so c₂ cancels.

misconceptions.feedback: That is c₂. The question asks for c₁.

questions.prompt: Do (1, 0) and (0, 0) form a basis for the plane?
hints: Can the pair reach every point? Is either vector wasted?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The zero vector is always redundant, and the pair only spans a line.

questions.onCorrect: The zero vector adds no direction, so the pair spans only a line.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero adds nothing. The pair spans only a line, so it cannot span the plane.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (2, 1) and (1, 2)?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare the ratio of up to across in each.
Independent vectors in the plane span a plane.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Neither vector is a multiple of the other, so they are independent and span a plane.

questions.onCorrect: Neither is a multiple of the other, so the pair is independent and spans a plane.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither vector is a multiple of the other, so both add a direction.

questions.prompt: Write (7, 3) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(2, 0). What is c₂?
hints: Which vector has an up part?
The second coordinates give c₁ on their own.
Use c₁ in the first coordinates, then solve for c₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate gives c₁ = 3; then 3 + 2c₂ = 7 gives c₂ = 2.

questions.onCorrect: Up coordinates give c₁. Then the across coordinates give c₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is c₁. Use it in the first coordinates to find c₂.
That stops before dividing by the first entry of the second vector.

questions.prompt: What is the rank of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Rank is the number of pivots.
Where does each row have its first nonzero entry?
Count the pivot columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is a pivot in the first and third columns, giving rank two.

questions.onCorrect: Rank is the number of pivots: columns 1 and 3 each have one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts all the columns. Rank counts only the pivot columns.

questions.prompt: What is the nullity of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Rank plus nullity equals the number of columns.
The matrix has three columns and rank two.
Take the rank away from the number of columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A has three columns and rank two, so nullity is 3 − 2 = 1.

questions.onCorrect: Three columns less rank two leaves nullity one: one free direction.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rank. Nullity is the number of columns minus the rank.
That counts all the columns. Take the rank away.

questions.prompt: Which of these vectors does A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ send to the zero vector?
hints: Apply A to each candidate, one row at a time.
A vector is sent to zero only if every output coordinate is zero.
Check the second row as well as the first.
questions.onCorrect: A(−2, 1, 0) = (−2 + 2 + 0, 0) = (0, 0). The products in the first row cancel and the second row picks out the third entry, which is 0, so the vector is sent to zero and lies in the null space.

misconceptions.feedback: A(2, 1, 0) = (2 + 2, 0) = (4, 0). The two products in the first row have the same sign, so they add instead of cancelling, and the output is not zero.
A(0, 0, 1) = (0, 1). The first output coordinate is 0, but the second is 1, and a vector is sent to zero only when every output coordinate is zero.

questions.prompt: Which pair of columns of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is a basis for its column space?
hints: Which columns hold the pivots?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Columns 1 and 3 hold the pivots. Column 2 is twice column 1.

questions.onCorrect: The pivot columns of the original matrix give a basis for the column space.

misconceptions.feedback: Column 2 is twice column 1, so that pair is redundant. Choose the pivot columns.

questions.prompt: What is the rank of $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Rank is the number of pivots.
Which diagonal entries are nonzero?
Count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three diagonal entries are nonzero, so there are three pivots.

questions.onCorrect: Each nonzero diagonal entry is a pivot, and there are three of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the diagonal entries. Rank counts the pivots.

questions.prompt: What is the nullity of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Is either row a multiple of the other?
Find the rank first, then take it away from the number of columns.
The matrix has three columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second row is redundant; rank is one and there are three columns, so nullity is two.

questions.onCorrect: The second row repeats the first, so the rank is one. Three columns less one is two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rank. Nullity is the number of columns minus the rank.
That counts all the columns. Take the rank away.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Multiply the main diagonal, then the other diagonal.
Subtract the second product from the first.
The determinant is ad − bc.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinant is 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts the second from the first.
Check the order: subtract bc from ad.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Multiply the main diagonal, then the other diagonal.
The second product is the larger one.
Subtract the second product from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinant is 1 × 1 − 3 × 2 = −5.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc = 1 − 6 = −5. Swapping the rows flipped the sign.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The second product is larger, so the result is negative.
That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts the second from the first.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Multiply the main diagonal, then the other diagonal.
Compare the two products.
Subtract the second from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The diagonal products are both 4, so their difference is zero.

questions.onCorrect: The columns are dependent, so the map flattens the plane and the determinant is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts the second from the first.

questions.prompt: A map scales lengths by 2 across, 3 up and 4 deep. A cube of volume 1 m³ becomes a box. What is the volume of the box, in cubic metres?
hints: Each direction is scaled on its own.
Volume is across times up times deep.
Multiply the three scales.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Multiply the diagonal scales: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: The box has sides 2, 3 and 4, so its volume is 2 × 3 × 4 = 24. Volume multiplies the three scale factors.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scales. Volume multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A = $\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. By what positive factor does A change area?
hints: Each direction is stretched on its own.
The flip does not change how big the area is.
Multiply the sizes of the two stretches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinant is −6. Its absolute value is the area factor 6.

questions.onCorrect: The determinant is −6. Its size, 6, is the area factor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the determinant. Area itself never goes negative, so use its size.

questions.prompt: A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. What is det(A B)?
hints: Find det(A) and det(B).
Determinants multiply when matrices multiply.
Multiply the two determinants.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinants are 6 and 2; det(A B) = 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: Doing one map after another multiplies the area factors: 6 × 2 = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two determinants. The determinant of a product is their product.

questions.prompt: Project (4, 2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Work out v · d and d · d.
Divide the first by the second to get the coefficient.
Multiply d by the coefficient and read the first entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficient is (4 + 2)/(1 + 1) = 3, so the projection is (3, 3).

questions.onCorrect: The coefficient is 6 ÷ 2. Scale d by it to land on the line.

misconceptions.feedback: That is v · d. Divide it by d · d, then scale d.
That is the x coordinate of v itself. Project first.

questions.prompt: Project (3, 4) onto the line spanned by (2, 0). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Which line is spanned by (2, 0)?
Projecting onto the x axis keeps the across position.
Read the across coordinate of the vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line is the x axis, so the projection keeps x = 3 and sets y = 0.

questions.onCorrect: The line is the x axis. Projecting keeps x and drops the height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the y coordinate of v. The x axis keeps x and drops y.
That is v · d. Divide it by d · d first.

questions.prompt: The projection of (4, 2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1) is (3, 3). What is the y coordinate of the residual, which is (4, 2) minus the projection?
hints: The residual is the vector minus its projection.
Subtract matching coordinates.
Subtract the projection's y coordinate from the vector's y coordinate, in that order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The residual is (4, 2) − (3, 3) = (1, −1), so its y coordinate is −1.

questions.onCorrect: The residual is (4, 2) − (3, 3) = (1, −1), so its y coordinate is −1. It is perpendicular to (1, 1), as every residual is.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the y coordinate of the projection. The residual is what is left when the projection is taken away from (4, 2).

questions.prompt: Project (2, −2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Work out v · d first.
What happens to a coefficient whose top is zero?
Zero times a direction is the zero vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Their dot product is zero, so the projection coefficient is zero.

questions.onCorrect: A vector perpendicular to the line has zero projection onto it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of v itself. Dot v with d first.

questions.prompt: Project (2, 5) onto the line spanned by (0, 1). What is the y coordinate?
hints: Which line is spanned by (0, 1)?
Projecting onto the y axis keeps the height.
Read the up coordinate of the vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line is the y axis, so the projection is (0, 5).

questions.onCorrect: The line is the y axis. Projecting keeps y and drops x.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of v. The y axis keeps y and drops x.

questions.prompt: Project (−2, 4) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Work out v · d and d · d.
Divide the first by the second.
Multiply d by the coefficient and read the first entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficient is (−2 + 4)/2 = 1, giving projection (1, 1).

questions.onCorrect: v · d = 2 and d · d = 2, so the coefficient is 1 and the projection is d itself.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of v itself. Project first.
That is v · d. Divide it by d · d, then scale d.

questions.prompt: Fit one constant to the measurements 2, 4 and 9 by least squares. What constant gives the smallest squared error?
hints: The measurements cannot all be matched. Balance them.
Use all three measurements.
Add them and divide by how many there are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is (2 + 4 + 9)/3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: For one constant, least squares gives the mean of the measurements.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle measurement. Use all three.
That is the total. Divide it by the number of measurements.

questions.prompt: Measurements 2, 4 and 9 are fitted by the constant 5. What is the sum of the residuals, measurement minus fit?
hints: Find each residual with its sign.
One of them is positive and two are negative.
Add the three residuals.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The residuals are −3, −1 and 4, whose sum is zero.

questions.onCorrect: The misses below and above cancel exactly, because the fit is the mean.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes and ignores the signs. Residuals can be negative.

questions.prompt: Fit y ≈ c + sx to the points (0, 1), (1, 2) and (2, 2) by least squares. What is s?
hints: The points are at equal steps across.
Use the slope shortcut: last y minus first y, over the number of steps.
Subtract the first y from the last y, then halve it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The normal equations are 3c + 3s = 5 and 3c + 5s = 6. Subtracting gives 2s = 1, so s = 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: (2 − 1) ÷ 2 = 0.5. The line cannot hit every point, so this slope balances the misses.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the last y minus the first. Divide by the number of steps across.

questions.prompt: Measurements 2, 4 and 9 are fitted by the constant 5. What is the sum of the squared residuals?
hints: Find each residual: measurement minus fit.
Square each residual.
Add the three squares.
questions.onCorrect: Squares make every miss positive: 9 + 1 + 16 = 26.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain sum of the residuals. Square each one first.

questions.prompt: Fit one constant by least squares to the measurements 1, 5 and 9. What is it?
hints: For one constant, the best fit is the mean.
Add the three measurements.
Divide the total by how many there are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Their mean is 15/3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: The mean of the measurements is the least-squares constant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total. Divide it by the number of measurements.

questions.prompt: The points (0, 2), (1, 5) and (2, 8) are fitted by the line y = c + sx. What is s?
hints: How much does y rise for each step in x?
Use the slope shortcut for points at 0, 1 and 2.
Subtract the first y from the last, then divide by the number of steps across.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The points lie exactly on y = 2 + 3x, so the least-squares slope is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The points lie exactly on y = 2 + 3x, so every residual is zero and the least-squares slope is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total rise. Divide it by the number of steps across.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of v = (1, 0) onto u = (1, 1). What is the y coordinate of the residual?
hints: Find the projection first.
The projection is the coefficient times u.
Subtract the projection's y from v's y.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The projection is (0.5, 0.5), so the residual is (0.5, −0.5).

questions.onCorrect: The residual is v minus the projection, and it is perpendicular to u.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. Subtract the projection's y from v's y, in that order.

questions.prompt: Normalise (1, 1). What is its first coordinate as a decimal?
hints: Find the length first.
Divide the first coordinate by that length.
Write the result as a decimal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The length is √2, so the first unit coordinate is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707107.

questions.onCorrect: The length is √2. Dividing 1 by √2 gives about 0.707107.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the coordinate before dividing by the length.
That multiplies by the length. Divide by it.

questions.prompt: Find (1, 1) · (1, −1), the dot product of the two directions.
hints: Multiply matching coordinates.
One product is negative.
Add the products.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products 1 and −1 cancel. Normalising both nonzero directions keeps their dot product zero.

questions.onCorrect: The products cancel, so the directions are perpendicular. Normalising keeps that.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes of the products. The second one is negative.

questions.prompt: For u = (1, 1) and v = (2, 2), can the residual of v create a second unit basis vector?
hints: Subtract the projection of v onto u. What is left?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. v lies along u, so its residual is the zero vector, which cannot be normalised.

questions.onCorrect: v lies along u, so the residual is zero. A zero vector cannot be normalised.

misconceptions.feedback: v is a multiple of u. Subtract its projection and nothing is left to normalise.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of (3, 1) onto (1, 0). What is the y coordinate of the residual?
hints: The projection onto the x axis keeps the across part.
Subtract it from the vector.
Only the up part is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The projection is (3, 0), leaving residual (0, 1).

questions.onCorrect: Remove the part along (1, 0) and only the up part remains.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of the residual. The question asks for y.
That is the x coordinate of v itself. Subtract the projection first.

questions.prompt: Normalise (−3, 4). What is the second coordinate?
hints: Find the length first.
Square both coordinates, add, then take the square root.
Divide the second coordinate by the length.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The length is 5, giving second coordinate 4/5 = 0.8.

questions.onCorrect: The length is 5, and 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the coordinate before dividing by the length.
That is the first coordinate. The question asks for the second.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1), find λ in A v = λv.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v.
Compare A v with v. What is the multiplier?
questions.onCorrect: A v = (3, 3) is 3 times v, so the eigenvalue is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a coordinate of v. Work out A v first, then compare.
That adds the two entries of A v. Compare A v with v instead.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, −1), find λ in A v = λv.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v, keeping the signs.
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A v = (1, −1), so this direction has eigenvalue 1.

questions.onCorrect: A v equals v, so this direction is left unchanged: eigenvalue 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second coordinate of v. The multiplier is the ratio of output to input.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 0), find λ.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v.
Compare A v with v. Check the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output is (−2, 0) = −2v.

questions.onCorrect: The output is −2 times v: the eigenvalue is negative, so the direction flips.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The output points opposite to the input.
That is the other diagonal entry, which acts on the y direction.

questions.prompt: Is (1, 0) an eigenvector of A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Work out A v. Is it on the same line as v?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. A(1, 0) = (2, 1), which is not a multiple of (1, 0).

questions.onCorrect: A v = (2, 1) is not a multiple of (1, 0), so (1, 0) is not an eigenvector.

misconceptions.feedback: A v comes out as (2, 1), which has an up part that v lacks. It is not a multiple of v.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (0, 1), find λ.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v.
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output is (0, 2) = 2v.

questions.onCorrect: The output is 2 times v. A diagonal matrix scales each axis by its own entry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the other diagonal entry, which acts on the x direction.

questions.prompt: A nonzero vector v satisfies A v = 0. Is v an eigenvector?
hints: Write A v = 0 in the form λv.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A v = 0 = 0v, so v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.

questions.onCorrect: A v = 0v, so v is an eigenvector. Only the vector v itself must be nonzero.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at A v = 0 again. Can it be written as a number times v?

questions.prompt: The first column of P is (1, 1) for A = $\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$. What is the first diagonal entry of D?
hints: D's entry is the eigenvalue of that column.
Work out A v for v = (1, 1).
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A(1, 1) = (6, 6) = 6(1, 1), so this column has eigenvalue 6 and D's first diagonal entry is 6.

questions.onCorrect: A(1, 1) = 6(1, 1), so the first diagonal entry of D is 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a coordinate of the eigenvector. D holds eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1), what scalar multiplies v in A²v?
hints: What is the eigenvalue of v?
Each application multiplies v by it.
Multiply by the eigenvalue twice.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The eigenvalue is 4, so applying the map twice gives 4²v = 16v.

questions.onCorrect: Two applications multiply by 4 twice: 4² = 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the eigenvalue. Applying the map twice multiplies by it twice.
That is the eigenvalue itself, which covers one application.

questions.prompt: A 2 × 2 matrix of real numbers has only one line of eigenvectors in the plane. Can it be diagonalised using real numbers?
hints: How many independent eigenvectors does P need?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. P needs two independent eigenvectors to be invertible.

questions.onCorrect: P needs a full set of independent eigenvectors. One direction is not enough in the plane.

misconceptions.feedback: P would need two independent eigenvector columns. With one direction it cannot be invertible.

questions.prompt: The first column of P is (1, −1) for A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. What is the first diagonal entry of D?
hints: D's entry is the eigenvalue of that column.
Work out A v for this v.
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: This direction has eigenvalue 1, so the first diagonal entry must be 1.

questions.onCorrect: The eigenvalue travels with its eigenvector, so D's entries reorder with P's columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the eigenvalue for the other direction. Each eigenvalue stays beside its own vector.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 0), what scalar multiplies v in A³v?
hints: What is the eigenvalue of v?
Each application multiplies v by it.
Multiply by the eigenvalue three times.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The eigenvalue is 2, so three applications multiply by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: Three applications multiply by 2 three times: 2³ = 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the eigenvalue by three. Applying the map three times raises it to the third power.

questions.prompt: In A = P D P⁻¹, why must P be invertible?
hints: What does an invertible matrix say about its columns?

acceptedIdeas: Its columns must form a basis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An invertible P has independent columns that span the space: a basis.

choices.label: Its columns must form a basis
Its columns must all be zero

questions.onCorrect: P is invertible exactly when its columns are a basis of eigenvectors.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero columns would make P collapse everything. P must be invertible.
The sign does not matter. It only has to be nonzero.

questions.prompt: What is the largest singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: The columns are perpendicular. How long is each?
Ignore the signs, because a flip is not a stretch.
Take the longer of the two lengths.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two stretch magnitudes are 3 and 2, so the largest singular value is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The stretch sizes are 3 and 2. The sign of the second is just a flip.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the smaller stretch. The question asks for the largest.

questions.prompt: For a 2 × 3 matrix A, what is the shape of Σ in the full SVD?
hints: Σ must map the same inputs to the same outputs as A.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Σ has the same shape as A: 2 × 3.

questions.onCorrect: Σ takes the same inputs to the same outputs, so it has A's shape.

misconceptions.feedback: That would drop an input. Σ takes the same three inputs as A to the same two outputs.
That would add an output. Σ has the same shape as A.

questions.prompt: What is the smaller singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: What is the rank of A?
The number of positive singular values equals the rank.
How many singular values does a two-by-two matrix have?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The matrix has rank one, so its second singular value is zero.

questions.onCorrect: Rank one means one positive singular value. The other is zero: the map flattens the plane to a line.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the larger singular value. The question asks for the smaller one.

questions.prompt: Which SVD factor performs the nonnegative stretching?
hints: Which factor is diagonal?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Σ holds the singular values. U and Vᵀ only turn.

questions.onCorrect: Σ is the diagonal stretch. U and Vᵀ preserve length.

misconceptions.feedback: U is orthogonal, so it only rotates or reflects.
Vᵀ is orthogonal, so it only rotates or reflects.

questions.prompt: What is the largest singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: The two columns are perpendicular. How long is each?
Ignore the zero row.
Take the longer of the two lengths.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The column directions are perpendicular with lengths 2 and 5; the largest stretch is 5.

questions.onCorrect: The columns are perpendicular, with lengths 2 and 5. The longest is the largest singular value.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the smaller stretch. The question asks for the largest.
That adds the two lengths. A stretch is measured along one direction.

questions.prompt: What is the smaller singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Which entries are the nonzero stretches?
Each row stretches along its own axis.
Take the smaller of the two stretches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two nonzero stretch factors are 2 and 1; the smaller is 1.

questions.onCorrect: The two nonzero stretches are 2 and 1, so the smaller singular value is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the larger singular value. The question asks for the smaller one.

questions.prompt: The move (2, 1) is followed by the move (−1, 3). How far up from its start does the path end?
hints: Which of the two moves went up?
Both did. Only the up parts count here.
Add the two up distances.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The up parts are 1 and 3, so 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The up parts are 1 and 3, which add to 4. The across parts do not enter into a question about how far up.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the up part of the second move alone. The first move went up as well, and the two up parts add.

hints: Add across to across, then up to up.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (7, 8): 5 + 2 across and 1 + 7 up.

questions.onCorrect: Each coordinate adds to the one in the same position: across with across, up with up.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds across to up. Each coordinate adds only to the one in the same position.
That multiplies the first coordinates. Adding vectors only adds.

questions.prompt: Why is the 2 applied to both coordinates of (3, 1)?
hints: Picture the arrow getting twice as long.

acceptedIdeas: Scaling stretches the whole vector, so every coordinate grows by the same factor.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stretching the whole arrow stretches both its across and up parts.

choices.label: Only the first coordinate changes when we scale.
The second coordinate must stay the same.
Scaling stretches the whole vector, so every coordinate grows by the same factor.

questions.onCorrect: A scalar stretches the whole arrow, so it multiplies every coordinate.

misconceptions.feedback: Then the arrow would change direction. Scaling keeps the direction, so both parts grow together.
Then the arrow would change direction. Both parts must grow by the same factor.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of 3(−1, 2) + (4, −5)?
hints: Scale the first vector before adding.
Multiply both entries of the first vector by the scalar, then add matching entries.
The first entry of the scaled vector is negative. Add the other vector's first entry to it.
questions.onCorrect: Scale first: 3 × (−1) = −3. Then add the matching entry, 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the second vector's entry instead of adding it.
That is the scaled entry alone. Add the other vector's entry.

questions.prompt: The vectors (1, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1) together span the whole plane. Which of them can be removed while the rest still span the whole plane?
hints: Which vector can be made from the other two?
After you remove one, are the remaining two independent?
Try removing a second vector and see what the rest can still reach.

acceptedIdeas: Any one of the three, but not two of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Any one of the three, because each is a combination of the other two, but not two of them, because one vector spans only a line.

choices.label: Any two of them, because one vector is enough
Only (1, 1), because it is the sum of the other two
None of them, because each one is needed
Any one of the three, but not two of them

questions.onCorrect: Each of the three is a combination of the other two, so any one can go and the remaining pair still spans the plane. A single vector spans only a line, so a second vector cannot be removed.

misconceptions.feedback: (1, 1) is the sum of the other two, but the relationship works in both directions: (1, 0) = (1, 1) − (0, 1), so (1, 0) can also be removed and the other two still span the plane.
Each of the three is a combination of the other two, so removing any one of them loses nothing and the remaining pair still spans the plane.
A single vector spans only a line, so removing two of the three leaves too little to reach the whole plane.

questions.prompt: How many vectors are in a basis for ordinary three-dimensional space?
hints: Every basis has as many vectors as the space has dimensions.
How many dimensions does ordinary space have?
Count the independent directions: across, up and one more.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ordinary space has three dimensions, so every basis has three vectors.

questions.onCorrect: A basis has as many vectors as the space has dimensions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of a basis for a plane. Ordinary space has a further direction.

questions.prompt: Why does a basis give each vector exactly one set of coordinates?
hints: There are two properties of a basis. Which gives existence, and which gives uniqueness?

acceptedIdeas: It spans, so every vector can be built, and it is independent, so there is only one way.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Spanning gives at least one way and independence gives at most one.

choices.label: Its vectors are always unit vectors.
It spans, so every vector can be built, and it is independent, so there is only one way.

questions.onCorrect: Spanning gives at least one way to build a vector. Independence allows at most one.

misconceptions.feedback: Basis vectors need not have length one. Spanning and independence do the work.
A basis can never contain the zero vector: it would be redundant.

questions.prompt: Write (8, 2) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1). What is c₂?
hints: Match the first coordinates, then the second.
You get two equations in c₁ and c₂.
Subtract the second equation from the first so that c₁ cancels.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equations are c₁ + c₂ = 8 and c₁ − c₂ = 2. Subtracting gives 2c₂ = 6, so c₂ = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Subtract the equations so c₁ cancels, then solve for c₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is c₁. The question asks for c₂.

questions.prompt: How far up is the part that remains?
hints: Which part of the vector lies along the x axis?
Cutting it off leaves only the up part.
Read the up coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Removing the across part leaves (0, 7), which is 7 up.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Subtracting a vector's part along a direction leaves the part perpendicular to it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the across part, which has been removed.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of (2, 3) onto e₁ = (1, 0). What is the y coordinate of the residual?
hints: The projection onto (1, 0) keeps the across part.
Subtract it from the vector.
Only the up part is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The projection is (2, 0), so the residual is (0, 3).

questions.onCorrect: The residual is (0, 3): the part perpendicular to e₁.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of the residual. The question asks for y.

questions.prompt: Why must we normalise the residual after subtracting?
hints: Which property does subtracting give, and which does it not?

acceptedIdeas: Subtracting makes it perpendicular, but it need not have length 1.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Subtraction gives a right angle with the first vector. Only dividing by the length gives length one.

choices.label: Subtracting makes it perpendicular, but it need not have length 1.
Subtracting makes it longer than before.
Subtracting makes it parallel to the first vector.

questions.onCorrect: Subtracting gives a right angle, not unit length. Dividing by the length finishes the job.

misconceptions.feedback: Length is not the issue. The residual may be shorter or longer. It just is not fixed at one.
The opposite: subtracting the projection leaves a vector at a right angle to the first.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of (2, 4) onto (1, 1). What is the x coordinate of the residual?
hints: Find the coefficient (v · d) ÷ (d · d).
Scale d by it to get the projection.
Subtract the projection's x from v's x.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficient is 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so the projection is (3, 3) and the residual is (−1, 1).

questions.onCorrect: The projection is (3, 3). Subtracting leaves (−1, 1), perpendicular to (1, 1).

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. Subtract the projection's x from v's x, in that order.
That is the projection's x coordinate. The residual is what is left.

questions.prompt: Machine P doubles a number and machine Q adds 3. A number goes through both machines, once with P first and once with Q first. Starting from 5, how do the two results compare?
hints: Work out each run in full.
With P first, double 5 and then add 3. With Q first, add 3 and then double.
Compare the two final numbers.

acceptedIdeas: P first gives 13 and Q first gives 16, so the order changes the result
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: P first gives 5 × 2 + 3 = 13 and Q first gives (5 + 3) × 2 = 16, so the order changes the result.

choices.label: Both orders give 16, because each machine does the same job whichever comes first
P first gives 13 and Q first gives 16, so the order changes the result
P first gives 16 and Q first gives 13, so the order changes the result

questions.onCorrect: With P first, 5 × 2 + 3 = 13, and with Q first, (5 + 3) × 2 = 16. The same two operations in a different order gave different results, which is why the order of a matrix product matters.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling 5 and then adding 3 gives 13, while adding 3 to 5 and then doubling gives 16, so the two orders do not agree.
With P first, 5 is doubled to 10 and then 3 is added, which gives 13. The machine that goes first changes the number that the second machine receives.

questions.prompt: To find entry (1, 1) of A B, which row and column do you pair?
hints: The left matrix gives the row. The right matrix gives the column.

acceptedIdeas: Row 1 of A with column 1 of B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Row i of A with column j of B, here with i = 1 and j = 1.

choices.label: Row 1 of A with column 1 of B
Row 1 of B with column 1 of A
Column 1 of A with row 1 of B

questions.onCorrect: Entry (i, j) of A B is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the order. The left matrix gives the row and the right matrix gives the column.
Rows of the left matrix pair with columns of the right matrix, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: Why do A B v and B A v give different results?
hints: Compare what the second map receives in each case.

acceptedIdeas: Each map acts on the output of the other, so the order changes what it acts on.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In one order B gets v, and in the other B gets A v. Different inputs, different outputs.

choices.label: Matrix multiplication only works one way round.
The vector v changes between the two.
Each map acts on the output of the other, so the order changes what it acts on.

questions.onCorrect: Each map receives a different input in each order, so the results usually differ.

misconceptions.feedback: Both products exist here. They are just different matrices.
The vector v is the same. What changes is what each map receives.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A B? Count from 1.
hints: Use the second row of A and the second column of B.
Multiply matching positions, then add.
The row is (2, 1). Dot it with the column.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Row (2, 1) dotted with column (1, 2) gives 2 + 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Row 2 of A dotted with column 2 of B: 2 × 1 + 1 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses column 1 of B. The question asks for column 2.

questions.prompt: A map stretches lengths across by 5 and lengths up by 2. A square tile with sides of 1 m becomes a rectangle. What is the area of the rectangle, in square metres?
hints: How long are the two sides of the rectangle?
Each side of the square is stretched on its own.
Area is across times up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sides become 5 m and 2 m, so the area is 5 × 2 = 10 m².

questions.onCorrect: The sides become 5 m and 2 m, so the area is 5 × 2 = 10 m². Area multiplies the two stretches.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two stretches. Area is across times up.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Multiply the main diagonal, then the other diagonal.
Subtract the second product from the first.
The determinant is ad − bc.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts the second from the first.
Check the order: subtract bc from ad.

questions.prompt: Why is the area factor 7 when the determinant is −7?
hints: What does the minus sign say about orientation?

acceptedIdeas: Area is never negative: the sign records a flip, and the size is the area factor.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The size 7 is how much area scales. The minus sign says the map flips orientation.

choices.label: Area is never negative: the sign records a flip, and the size is the area factor.
The sign can be ignored because determinants are always positive.
Area factors are always between zero and one.

questions.onCorrect: The sign records a flip. The size of the determinant is the area factor.

misconceptions.feedback: Determinants can be negative, as this one is. The sign carries meaning: a flip.
A map can stretch area as well as shrink it. This one stretches area by seven.

questions.prompt: A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&-3\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$. By what positive factor does A change area?
hints: Find the determinant first.
The second diagonal product has a negative entry.
Take the size of the determinant.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinant is 1 × 2 − (−3) × 2 = 8, so area scales by 8.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc = 2 − (−6) = 8. The area factor is its size.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign of bc: one of its entries is negative, so subtracting it adds.

questions.prompt: A matrix triples every vector along (1, 1) and leaves every vector along (1, −1) unchanged. What is the first coordinate of its output for the vector (2, 0)?
hints: Split (2, 0) into its two parts.
One part is tripled and the other is unchanged.
Add the two outputs, then read the first coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output is 3(1, 1) + (1, −1) = (4, 2), so the first coordinate is 4.

questions.onCorrect: (2, 0) = (1, 1) + (1, −1), so the output is 3(1, 1) + (1, −1) = (4, 2), and its first coordinate is 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That triples the whole vector. Only the part along (1, 1) is tripled.
That is the first coordinate of the input. The matrix changes one of the two parts.

questions.prompt: In A = P D P⁻¹, the first column of P is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 7. What is the first diagonal entry of D?
hints: D holds the eigenvalues.
They sit in the same order as the columns of P.
Read the eigenvalue of the first column.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: D's first diagonal entry is the eigenvalue of P's first column, which is 7.

questions.onCorrect: D lists the eigenvalues in the same order as the columns of P.

misconceptions.feedback: That squares the eigenvalue. D holds the eigenvalues themselves.

questions.prompt: Why does applying A twice multiply an eigenvector by λ²?
hints: What does one application do to an eigenvector?

acceptedIdeas: Each application multiplies the vector by λ again.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A v = λv, and applying A to λv gives λ times A v, which is λ²v.

choices.label: The second application cancels the first.
Each application multiplies the vector by λ again.

questions.onCorrect: Each application scales by λ again, so after two applications the factor is λ².

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing cancels: the vector is scaled again, so the scale factors multiply.
A² keeps every eigenvector of A. It just squares each eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (0, 1), what scalar multiplies v in A⁴v?
hints: What is the eigenvalue of v?
Each application multiplies v by it.
Multiply by the eigenvalue four times, watching the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The eigenvalue is −2, so A⁴v = (−2)⁴v = 16v.

questions.onCorrect: (−2)⁴ = 16. An even power of a negative eigenvalue is positive.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the third power. Apply the map four times.
That is the eigenvalue itself, which covers one application.

questions.prompt: A rectangular field is 9 m wide and 12 m long. How many metres is it straight across from one corner to the opposite corner?
hints: Draw the rectangle. The line straight across is the long side of a right-angled triangle.
Pythagoras: square the two short sides and add the squares.
Which number multiplied by itself gives that total?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The squares are 81 and 144, which sum to 225. The square root of 225 is 15.

questions.onCorrect: Square the sides, add, take the square root. That is exactly how a vector's length works.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the two sides added: the way round. The straight route is shorter.
That is the sum of the squares. The distance is its square root.

hints: Multiply the first entries, multiply the second entries, then add.
questions.onCorrect: Multiply matching entries, then add the products: 3 + 8 gives one number.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the two products, but a dot product adds them into one number.
That adds all four entries. Multiply the matching pairs first.

questions.prompt: Why does the minus sign on −7 not matter once it is squared?
hints: What is a negative number times itself?

acceptedIdeas: A negative number squared is positive.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A negative times a negative is positive, so (−7)² = 49.

choices.label: Squaring a number removes its size.
A negative number squared is positive.
Minus signs never matter in vectors.

questions.onCorrect: A negative times a negative is positive, so squaring hides the sign. Length ignores direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The size stays: 7 squared is 49. Only the sign changes.
They matter a great deal in coordinates. They stop mattering here only because squaring makes a number positive.

hints: Multiply matching coordinates.
The first product is negative and the second is positive.
Add the two products, keeping their signs.
questions.onCorrect: −6 + 20 = 14. Keep each product's sign, then add.

misconceptions.feedback: The first product is (−2) × 3, which is negative. Keep its sign.

questions.prompt: A matrix sends the vector (1, 2) to the vector (4, 8), which lies on the same line. By what number did it multiply (1, 2)?
hints: Compare the output with the input, one coordinate at a time.
Is each output coordinate the same multiple of the input one?
Divide an output coordinate by the matching input coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (4, 8) = 4(1, 2), so the multiplier is 4.

questions.onCorrect: (4, 8) = 4(1, 2), so the multiplier is 4. When the output lies on the input's line, the ratio of output to input is the eigenvalue.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how much the first coordinate grew by. Compare by multiplying, not adding.

questions.prompt: A v = 6v for v = (1, 2). What is the first coordinate of A v?
hints: A v is v scaled by the eigenvalue.
Multiply each coordinate of v by the eigenvalue.
Read the first coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A v = 6(1, 2) = (6, 12), so the first coordinate is 6.

questions.onCorrect: A v = λv, so each coordinate of v is multiplied by λ.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of v itself. A v is v scaled.
That is the second coordinate of A v. The question asks for the first.

questions.prompt: Why is (1, 1) an eigenvector of the matrix with rows (4, 1) and (2, 3)?
hints: What is the test for an eigenvector?

acceptedIdeas: A v is a scalar multiple of v, so the output stays on the same line.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The output (5, 5) is a multiple of (1, 1).

choices.label: A v is a scalar multiple of v, so the output stays on the same line.
The matrix has no negative entries.

questions.onCorrect: An eigenvector's output is a multiple of itself, so it stays on its own line.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a feature of this vector, not the test. The test compares A v with v.
Signs do not decide it. The test is whether A v is a multiple of v.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, −1), find λ.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v, keeping the signs.
Compare A v with v. Check the sign.
questions.onCorrect: The output is the negative of v, so the eigenvalue is −1.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The output points opposite to the input.
That is the scale factor for a different direction.

questions.prompt: What single value, in centimetres, is the fairest to report?
hints: The three readings disagree. How can you balance them?
Use all three, not just the middle one.
Add them and share the total equally.
questions.onCorrect: 8 cm. Averaging balances the readings. That mean is the least-squares constant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle reading. Use all three measurements.
That is the total. Share it between the three readings.

questions.prompt: Three readings of one quantity are 1, 2 and 6. Project the vector of readings (1, 2, 6) onto (1, 1, 1). What single value x results?
hints: Which direction are the three readings projected onto?
Dot the readings with (1, 1, 1), and dot (1, 1, 1) with itself.
Divide the first number by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The coefficient is (1 + 2 + 6)/3 = 3, so the nearest single value to the three readings is their mean, 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle reading. Project all three readings, not just one.
That is the total of the readings. Divide it by the number of readings.

questions.prompt: Why do the residuals of a least-squares constant add up to zero?
hints: Which direction is the residual column perpendicular to, and what does that say about a dot product with it?

acceptedIdeas: The residuals are perpendicular to (1, 1, 1), so their entries add up to zero.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The residual column is perpendicular to (1, 1, 1), so its entries sum to zero.

choices.label: The residuals are perpendicular to (1, 1, 1), so their entries add up to zero.

questions.onCorrect: The residual column is perpendicular to (1, 1, 1), so its entries sum to zero: errors above and below balance.

misconceptions.feedback: Only when every measurement is matched. Here they are not: each residual is a miss.
The sum is taken before squaring. Squares are used afterwards to measure total error.

questions.prompt: Fit y ≈ c + sx to the points (0, 4), (1, 3) and (2, 0) by least squares. What is s?
hints: Does y rise or fall as x grows?
Use the slope shortcut: last y minus first y, over the number of steps.
Subtract the first y from the last y, then halve it.
questions.onCorrect: The y values fall, so the slope is negative: (0 − 4) ÷ 2 = −2.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The points fall as x grows.
That is the last y minus the first. Divide by the number of steps across.

questions.prompt: A machine doubles a number and then adds 3, and it gave back 17. What number went in?
hints: The machine did two things. Undo them in the opposite order.
Undo the adding first.
Take away the added amount, then undo the doubling.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 17 − 3 = 14, and half of 14 is 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. You undid the last step first, then the one before it. An inverse map does just that.

misconceptions.feedback: That only undoes the adding. The doubling has to be undone as well.

questions.prompt: What does A⁻¹ A equal?
hints: The inverse undoes A. What is left when nothing happens?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A⁻¹ A = I: undoing A leaves every vector unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: Undoing A leaves every vector unchanged, which is what the identity matrix does.

misconceptions.feedback: A⁻¹ undoes A, so nothing of A is left. The result leaves every vector unchanged.
The zero matrix would send every vector to zero. Undoing a map leaves vectors as they were.

questions.prompt: Why is there no inverse when ad − bc = 0?
hints: Look at the last step of the formula.

acceptedIdeas: The formula divides by ad − bc, and you cannot divide by zero.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The inverse is built by dividing by ad − bc, which fails when it is zero.

choices.label: The zero matrix cannot be multiplied.
The formula divides by ad − bc, and you cannot divide by zero.
A matrix with a zero entry never has an inverse.

questions.onCorrect: The formula divides by ad − bc, so a zero there means no inverse.

misconceptions.feedback: Many matrices with zero entries have inverses. The test is the number ad − bc.
Any matrices of matching shape can be multiplied. The issue is the division in the formula.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: Find ad − bc first.
The off-diagonal entries change sign.
Negate the entry in the top right of A, then divide by ad − bc.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ad − bc = 4 − 3 = 1, so the inverse is [(2, −3); (−1, 2)] and the entry is −3.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc is 1, and the off-diagonal entry is negated: −3.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The off-diagonal entries are negated.

questions.prompt: A rule sends the point (x, y) to the point (2x + y, y). What is the first coordinate of the point that (3, 1) is sent to?
hints: Which value goes in for x, and which for y?
2x means 2 times x.
Work out 2 times the x value, then add the y value.
questions.onCorrect: The first coordinate is 2x + y with x = 3 and y = 1, which is 6 + 1 = 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers instead of using 2x as 2 times x.

questions.prompt: The rule (x, y) → (3x + y, x + 2y) sends (1, 1) to (4, 3). What does it send (3, 3) to?
hints: How is (3, 3) related to (1, 1)?
Apply the rule to (3, 3) directly to check.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (3, 3) is three times (1, 1), and the output is three times (4, 3), which is (12, 9).

questions.onCorrect: Tripling the input tripled the output, which is the scaling law that the next screen states for every linear map.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 3 to each coordinate of (4, 3). The rule gives 3 × 3 + 3 = 12 and 3 + 2 × 3 = 9, which is three times (4, 3).
(3, 3) is a different input from (1, 1), and the rule gives 3 × 3 + 3 = 12 for its first coordinate.

questions.prompt: Why does the input (1, 0) pick out the first column of a matrix?
hints: What happens to an entry that is multiplied by zero?

acceptedIdeas: Each row's second entry is multiplied by 0, so only the first entry is left.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero kills the second entry of every row, leaving the first entries: the first column.

choices.label: Each row's second entry is multiplied by 0, so only the first entry is left.
The input (1, 0) is always the largest vector.

questions.onCorrect: The zero in the input wipes out every row's second entry, leaving the first column.

misconceptions.feedback: Size has nothing to do with it. Look at what the zero in the input multiplies.
Only when the first column is zero. In general the first column is the output.

questions.prompt: A linear map T sends (1, 0) to (2, 5) and (0, 1) to (1, −1). What is the first coordinate of T(3, 2)?
hints: Write (3, 2) as 3 lots of (1, 0) plus 2 lots of (0, 1).
A linear map keeps scaling and sums.
Combine the scaled outputs, then read the first entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T(3, 2) = 3(2, 5) + 2(1, −1) = (8, 13), so the first coordinate is 8.

questions.onCorrect: T(3, 2) = 3T(1, 0) + 2T(0, 1). The two column outputs are all you need.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second coordinate of the output. The question asks for the first.

questions.prompt: A timetable has 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side. You flip it so that the days run down the side. What does the flipped timetable have?
hints: Which direction do the periods run in the original timetable?
Flipping swaps the across and down directions.
There are still 4 days and 7 periods after the flip. Only the direction each one runs in has changed.

acceptedIdeas: 7 periods across the top and 4 days down the side
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 7 periods across the top and 4 days down the side, because flipping swaps the two directions and keeps each count with its own label.

choices.label: 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side
7 periods across the top and 4 days down the side
4 periods across the top and 7 days down the side

questions.onCorrect: The 7 periods move from the side to the top and the 4 days move from the top to the side. A matrix transpose does the same to rows and columns, exchanging the two directions and keeping each count with its own label.

misconceptions.feedback: The counts belong to what is being counted. There are 4 days and 7 periods, and flipping moves each kind to the other direction without changing how many there are.
That is the original timetable. Once the days run down the side, the periods have to run across the top.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5&6&7\\8&9&0\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Count the rows first, then the columns.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has 2 rows and 3 columns, so its shape is 2 × 3.

questions.onCorrect: Rows first, then columns: 2 rows and 3 columns make shape 2 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shape of its transpose. Count rows first, then columns.
That counts all the entries. Shape is the number of rows by the number of columns.

questions.prompt: Why does entry (2, 3) of A end up at position (3, 2) in Aᵀ?
hints: Which of the two numbers in the position does the transpose change?

acceptedIdeas: Transposing swaps each entry's row and column.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Row i becomes column i, so every entry swaps its row and column.

choices.label: Transposing changes the sign of each entry.
Transposing swaps each entry's row and column.
Transposing reverses the order of all the entries.

questions.onCorrect: Row i becomes column i, so each entry's row and column numbers swap.

misconceptions.feedback: Reversing everything would also change the row. The transpose keeps each entry and swaps only its position's two numbers.
The entries stay as they are. Only their positions change.

questions.prompt: Let C = $\begin{pmatrix}5&8\\6&9\\7&4\end{pmatrix}$. What is entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ comes from entry (3, 2) of C.
Look in the third row and the second column of C.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ is entry (3, 2) of C, which is 4.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the positions: entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ is entry (3, 2) of C.

misconceptions.feedback: That is entry (2, 2) of C. Check the row and column numbers after swapping.
That is entry (1, 2) of C. Check the row and column numbers after swapping.

questions.prompt: Two numbers x and y are required to satisfy x + y = 4 and 2x + 2y = 9 at the same time. Which statement is true?
hints: How are the two left-hand sides related?
Double the first equation.
Compare what you get with the second equation.

acceptedIdeas: No pair works, because doubling the first equation gives 2x + 2y = 8, which contradicts the second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No pair works, because doubling the first equation gives 2x + 2y = 8, which contradicts 2x + 2y = 9.

choices.label: No pair works, because doubling the first equation gives 2x + 2y = 8, which contradicts the second
Exactly one pair works, because there are two equations for two unknowns
Infinitely many pairs work, because the second equation is a multiple of the first

questions.onCorrect: Twice the first equation says 2x + 2y = 8, which contradicts 2x + 2y = 9, so no pair satisfies both.

misconceptions.feedback: The second equation is a multiple of the first only if its right side is multiplied as well. Twice 4 is 8 and the second equation says 9, so the equations disagree.
Two equations for two unknowns give a single solution only when the lines cross. These lines are parallel, since the left sides are in the ratio 1 to 2 and the right sides, 4 and 9, are not.

questions.prompt: A row of a reduced system reads 0 = 5. What does that tell you about the system?
hints: Can any values of the unknowns make zero equal five?
A row is an equation that every solution must satisfy.
What does an impossible equation do to the whole system?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has no solution, because 0 = 5 is false whatever the unknowns are.

choices.label: It has exactly one solution, in which every unknown is 0
It has infinitely many solutions, because the row puts no restriction on the unknowns

questions.onCorrect: Every solution has to satisfy every row, and 0 = 5 is false whatever the unknowns are, so the system has no solution.

misconceptions.feedback: The row says 0x₁ + 0x₂ = 5, which is false for every choice of the unknowns, including setting all of them to 0, so no solution of any kind exists.
A row that reads 0 = 0 puts no restriction on the unknowns, but this row reads 0 = 5, and no values of the unknowns can make that true.

questions.prompt: Why does a row reading 0 = 1 mean there is no solution?
hints: Every solution must satisfy every row.

acceptedIdeas: No values of the unknowns can make zero equal one.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every solution must satisfy every row, and no values make 0 = 1 true.

choices.label: No values of the unknowns can make zero equal one.
The system has more unknowns than equations.
The unknowns must all be zero.

questions.onCorrect: Every solution must satisfy every row. No values make 0 = 1 true.

misconceptions.feedback: If all the unknowns were zero, the row would still read 0 = 1. It is false whatever the values.
That can happen with solutions too. This row fails for a different reason: it is simply false.

questions.prompt: A consistent system has 5 unknowns, and its reduced form has 2 pivots. How many free variables does it have?
hints: Free variables are the unknowns without a pivot.
Count the unknowns, then take away the pivots.
Subtract the number of pivots from the number of unknowns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 unknowns less 2 pivots leaves 3 free variables.

questions.onCorrect: Unknowns minus pivots: 5 − 2 leaves 3 free variables.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pivots. Free variables are the unknowns left over.

questions.prompt: A step of (6, 8) metres is 10 m long. By what number do you multiply it to get a step of 1 m in the same direction?
hints: How long is the step now?
You must shrink the length down to the wanted one. What fraction of the length is that?
Divide the wanted length by the current length.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The step is 10 m long and should be 1 m, so multiply by 1/10 = 0.1.

questions.onCorrect: 0.1. Scaling by one over the length gives length 1 and keeps the direction.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the length, which makes the step ten times longer.

questions.prompt: Which pair of vectors is orthogonal?
hints: Find each pair's dot product. Which one gives zero?
questions.onCorrect: Orthogonal means a dot product of zero: 1 − 1 = 0.

misconceptions.feedback: Their dot product is not zero: the products 2 and 6 add up.
Their dot product is not zero: both products are positive, so they cannot cancel.

questions.prompt: Why do we divide by the length to make a unit vector?
hints: Think what dividing by a number does to every coordinate.

acceptedIdeas: Dividing by the length shrinks the vector to length 1 without turning it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dividing every coordinate by the same positive number shrinks the arrow and keeps its direction.

choices.label: Dividing by the length removes its minus signs.
Dividing by the length makes the vector orthogonal.
Dividing by the length shrinks the vector to length 1 without turning it.

questions.onCorrect: A positive scalar shrinks the arrow without turning it. Dividing by the length makes it exactly 1.

misconceptions.feedback: Orthogonal is about two vectors meeting at a right angle. Scaling one vector never turns it.
Signs stay: the length is positive, so each coordinate keeps its sign.

questions.prompt: A unit vector in the direction (8, −6) has what x coordinate?
hints: Find the length first.
Square each coordinate and add. The length is the root of that sum.
Divide the x coordinate by that length, as a decimal.
questions.onCorrect: The length is √(64 + 36) = 10. Then 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the coordinate before dividing by the length.
That is the size of the y coordinate. The question asks for x.

questions.prompt: A point is 6 units across and 5 units up. Dropping it straight down onto the line along the across direction, how far along that line does it land?
hints: Which part of the position is along the line?
Dropping straight down changes the height only.
Read the across coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dropping straight down keeps the across distance, so it lands at 6.
